Dickies").[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-174)

The Ramones' [eponymous debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones_(album) "Ramones (album)") had an outsized effect relative to its modest sales, particularly in the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). According to [Generation X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_X_(band) "Generation X (band)") bassist [Tony James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_James_(musician) "Tony James (musician)"), "Everybody went up three gears the day they got that first Ramones album. Punk rock—that rama-lama super fast stuff—is totally down to the Ramones. Bands were just playing in an [MC5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MC5 "MC5") groove until then."[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-175) His bandmate, [Billy Idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Idol "Billy Idol"), reiterated this saying that except for the [Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols"), every London punk band started speeding up their music up after hearing the Ramones.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-176) While Sex Pistols drummer [Paul Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Cook "Paul Cook") denied a musical influence, he credits the release of the first Ramones album as motivating the Pistols.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-177)

The Ramones' two July 1976 shows, like their debut album, are seen as having a significant impact on the style of many of the newly formed British punk acts—as one observer put it, "instantly nearly every band speeded up".[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-178) The Ramones' first British concert, at London's Roundhouse music venue, was held on July 4, 1976, the [United States Bicentennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Bicentennial "United States Bicentennial").[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-179) The Sex Pistols were playing in [Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheffield "Sheffield") that evening, supported by [the Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clash "The Clash"), making their public debut. The next night, members of both bands attended the Ramones' gig at the Dingwall's club. Ramones manager Danny Fields recalls a conversation between Johnny Ramone and Clash bassist [Paul Simonon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Simonon "Paul Simonon") (which he mislocates at the Roundhouse): "Johnny asked him, 'What do you do? Are you in a band?' Paul said, 'Well, we just rehearse. We call ourselves the Clash but we're not good enough.' Johnny said, 'Wait till you see us—we stink, we're lousy, we can't play. Just get out there and do it.'"[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-180) Another band whose members saw the Ramones perform on the 4th, [the Damned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Damned_(band) "The Damned (band)"), played [their first show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_at_the_100_Club_(The_Damned_album) "Live at the 100 Club (The Damned album)") two days later.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-181)

Other U.K. punk bands who were influenced during this period include [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_(band) "Chelsea (band)"),[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-182)[the Lurkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lurkers "The Lurkers"),[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-183)[the Undertones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Undertones "The Undertones"),[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-184) and [The Vibrators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vibrators "The Vibrators").[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-185)[Jimmy Pursey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Pursey "Jimmy Pursey") of [Sham 69](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sham_69 "Sham 69") has said that he considers the Ramones his band's "only blueprint".[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-186) The central [fanzine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanzine "Fanzine") of the early UK punk scene, _[Sniffin' Glue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sniffin'\_Glue "Sniffin' Glue")_, was named after the song "Now I Wanna Sniff Some Glue", which appeared on the debut LP.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-DG-187)

The Ramones' pop-influenced style of punk rock has been credited for paving the way for the birth of [pop-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-punk "Pop-punk"),[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-188) being cited as an influence by those of [Green Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Day "Green Day"), [the Offspring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Offspring "The Offspring"), [Blink-182](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blink-182 "Blink-182"),[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-189)[Fall Out Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_Out_Boy "Fall Out Boy"),[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-190)[New Found Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Found_Glory "New Found Glory"),[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-191) and [Alkaline Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_Trio "Alkaline Trio").[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-192) Green Day frontman [Billie Joe Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Joe_Armstrong "Billie Joe Armstrong") named his son Joey in homage to Joey Ramone, and drummer [Tré Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%A9_Cool "Tré Cool") named his daughter Ramona.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-193) The [Riverdales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverdales "Riverdales"), who Armstrong produced, emulated the sound of the Ramones throughout their career.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-194)

### Other genres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Other genres")]

The Ramones also influenced musicians associated with genres outside of punk, such as [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music"). Their influence on metal gave birth to the punk-metal "fusion" genre of [thrash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrash_metal "Thrash metal"). [Metallica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallica "Metallica") guitarist [Kirk Hammett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Hammett "Kirk Hammett"), one of the originators of thrash guitar, has described the importance of Johnny's rapid-fire guitar playing style to his own musical development.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-195)[Motörhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mot%C3%B6rhead "Motörhead") lead singer [Lemmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemmy "Lemmy"), a friend of the Ramones since the late 1970s, mixed the band's "Go Home Ann" in 1985. The members of Motörhead later composed the song "[R.A.M.O.N.E.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R.A.M.O.N.E.S. "R.A.M.O.N.E.S.")" as a tribute, and Lemmy performed at the final Ramones concert in 1996.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-196)[Paul Di'Anno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Di'Anno "Paul Di'Anno"), who sang on [Iron Maiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Maiden "Iron Maiden")'s first two albums called the Ramones his "favorite band", and often performed Ramones material in his live shows.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-197)[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-198) In the realm of [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock"), the song "[53rd & 3rd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/53rd_&_3rd_(song) "53rd & 3rd (song)")" lent its name to a British [indie pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_pop "Indie pop") label cofounded by Stephen Pastel of the Scottish band [the Pastels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pastels "The Pastels"), and [Morrissey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrissey "Morrissey"), while initially giving a negative review to the Ramones debut album, later commented, "three days after writing that Ramones piece, I realized that my love for the Ramones would out-live time itself."[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-199) In 2014, he was invited by the band's management to pick the tracks for a compilation that became _[Morrissey Curates The Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrissey\_Curates\_The\_Ramones "Morrissey Curates The Ramones")._[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-200)

### Accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Accolades")]

In 2000, [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1")'s _100 Greatest Artists of Hard Rock_ ranked the group at 17 on their list.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In addition to their 2002 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the Ramones were inducted into the [Long Island Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Music_Hall_of_Fame "Long Island Music Hall of Fame") in 2007.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-220) That October saw the release of a DVD set containing concert footage of the band: _[It's Alive 1974–1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_Alive\_1974%E2%80%931996 "It's Alive 1974–1996")_ includes 118 songs from 33 performances over the span of the group's career.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-221) In February 2011 the group was honored with a [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award"). Drummers Tommy, Marky, and Richie attended the ceremony.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-Sterndan-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-grammy1-14) Marky declared, "This is amazing. I never expected this. I'm sure Johnny, Joey, and Dee Dee would never have expected this."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-Sterndan-13) Richie noted that it was the first time ever that all three drummers were under the same roof, and mused that he couldn't "help thinking that [Joey] is watching us right now with a little smile on his face behind his rose-colored glasses."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-grammy1-14) On April 30, 2014, their debut album, _[Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones\_(album) "Ramones (album)")_, became certified Gold by the [Recording Industry of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_of_America "Recording Industry of America") (RIAA) after selling 500,000 copies, 38 years after its release.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-222)

The band members were also individually influential. [Johnny Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Ramone "Johnny Ramone") was named one of [_Time_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")'s "10 Greatest Electric-Guitar Players" in 2003.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-223) That same year, he was number 16 on the "100 Greatest Guitarists of All Time" list in _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-224) On November 30, 2003, New York City unveiled a sign designating East 2nd Street at the corner of Bowery as Joey Ramone Place. The singer lived on East 2nd for a time, and the sign is near the former Bowery site of [CBGB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBGB "CBGB").[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones#cite_note-225)

The French animated series _[Oggy and the Cockroaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oggy\_and\_the\_Cockroaches "Oggy and the Cockroaches")_ features a trio of anthropomorphic cockroaches named after three members of the band — Joey, Marky and Dee Dee.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[Bob Daisley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Daisley "Bob Daisley") and drummer [Lee Kerslake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kerslake "Lee 200").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) Singles "[Crazy Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Train "Crazy Train")" and "[Mr Crowley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr_Crowley "Mr Crowley")" reached the top 50 of the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5) and the album has been certified four times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-RIAA-6) 1981's _[Diary of a Madman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary\_of\_a\_Madman\_(album) "Diary of a Madman (album)")_ reached the top 20 in the UK, Canada and the US,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-CANstudio-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) and was certified triple platinum by the RIAA.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-RIAA-6) The album was the last to feature Daisley and Kerslake, Osbourne of whom were fired from Black Sabbath and replaced by [Ronnie James Dio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_James_Dio "Ronnie James Dio"), respectively, as well as the last to feature Rhoads, who died in a plane crash on 19 March 1982.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-allmusic-1)

Osbourne's first live album _[Speak of the Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_of\_the\_Devil\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Speak of the Devil (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_, featuring touring guitarist [Brad Gillis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Gillis "Brad Gillis"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-7) reached number 21 in the UK and number 14 in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4)[Jake E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_E._Lee "Jake E. Lee") joined in 1983, with _[Bark at the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bark\_at\_the\_Moon "Bark at the Moon")_ released later in the year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-allmusic-1) The album reached number 24 in the UK and number 19 in the US,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) spawning UK top 40 singles "[Bark at the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bark_at_the_Moon_(song) "Bark at the Moon (song)")" and "[So Tired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Tired_(Ozzy_Osbourne_song) "So Tired (Ozzy Osbourne song)")".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5)_[The Ultimate Sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ultimate\_Sin "The Ultimate Sin")_ followed in 1986, reaching the top ten in the UK and the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) Lead single "[Shot in the Dark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shot_in_the_Dark_(Ozzy_Osbourne_song) "Shot in the Dark (Ozzy Osbourne song)")" reached number 20 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") and number 68 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US100-8) The 1987 live album _[Tribute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribute\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Tribute (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_ charted in the top 20 in the UK and the top ten in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) After Lee was replaced by [Zakk Wylde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zakk_Wylde "Zakk Wylde"), _[No Rest for the Wicked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_Rest\_for\_the\_Wicked\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "No Rest for the Wicked (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_ was released in 1988 and reached number 23 in the UK and number 13 in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) The following year, Osbourne reached the top ten of the Hot 100 with [Lita Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lita_Ford "Lita Ford") on "[Close My Eyes Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_My_Eyes_Forever "Close My Eyes Forever")", peaking at number 8.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-USfeatured-9) 1991's _[No More Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_More\_Tears "No More Tears")_ reached the UK top 20,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2) the US top ten,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) and was certified four times platinum by the RIAA.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-RIAA-6) Singles "[No More Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_More_Tears_(Ozzy_Osbourne_song) "No More Tears (Ozzy Osbourne song)")" and "[Mama, I'm Coming Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mama,_I'm_Coming_Home "Mama, I'm Coming Home")" both reached the UK top 50 and charted on the _Billboard_ Hot 100.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US100-8) In 1992, Osbourne reached the UK Singles Chart top ten for the first time with [Was (Not Was)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Was_(Not_Was) "Was (Not Was)") and [Kim Basinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Basinger "Kim Basinger") on "[Shake Your Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake_Your_Head "Shake Your Head")", which peaked at number 4.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKfeatured-10)

After briefly retiring,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-allmusic-1) Osbourne returned with _[Ozzmosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzmosis "Ozzmosis")_ in 1995, which was his first album to reach the top five of the _Billboard_ 200 when it peaked at number 4.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) Lead single "Perry Mason" reached number 23 on the UK Singles Chart.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5) 1997 compilation _[The Ozzman Cometh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ozzman\_Cometh "The Ozzman Cometh")_ reached the US top 20 and was certified double platinum.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-RIAA-6) In 2001 he released _[Down to Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down\_to\_Earth\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Down to Earth (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_, which reached number 19 in the UK and number 4 in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) The album spawned the successful single "[Dreamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamer_(Ozzy_Osbourne_song) "Dreamer (Ozzy Osbourne song)")", which was certified gold in Austria and Germany.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-IFPIAUT-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-BVMI-12) In 2003, Osbourne collaborated with daughter [Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Osbourne "Kelly Osbourne") on a recording of Black Sabbath's "[Changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changes_(Black_Sabbath_song) "Changes (Black Sabbath song)")", which was both artists' first (and to date, only) number-one single in the UK.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5)_[The Essential Ozzy Osbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Essential\_Ozzy\_Osbourne "The Essential Ozzy Osbourne")_ was released the same year, reaching number 21 in the UK.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2) In 2005, Osbourne released an album of [cover versions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") entitled _[Under Cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under\_Cover\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Under Cover (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-13) which charted in the UK at number 67.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2) 2007's _[Black Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Rain\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Black Rain (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_ reached number 8 in the UK and number 3 in the US, while 2010's _[Scream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scream\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Scream (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_ reached number 12 in the UK and number 4 in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) The compilation _[Memoirs Of A Madman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoirs\_of\_a\_Madman\_(album) "Memoirs of a Madman (album)")_ charted in the UK at number 23 in 2014.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)

As of 2014, Osbourne has sold more than 100 million albums worldwide, including those during his time in Black Sabbath.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-15)

The [discography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discography "Discography") of [Ozzy Osbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne "Ozzy Osbourne"), an English [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music") singer, consists of 13 [studio albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album "Album"), five [live albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_album "Live album"), seven [compilation albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_album "Compilation album"), five [extended plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") (EPs), 65 [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(music) "Single (music)"), nine [video albums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video "Video") and 41 [music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video"). After being fired from Black Sabbath in 1979, Osbourne started his solo career with a band consisting of guitarist [Randy Rhoads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randy_Rhoads "Randy Rhoads"), bassist [Bob Daisley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Daisley "Bob Daisley") and drummer [Lee Kerslake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kerslake "Lee Kerslake").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-allmusic-1) The group released their debut album _[Blizzard of Ozz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blizzard\_of\_Ozz "Blizzard of Ozz")_ in 1980, which reached number 7 on the [UK Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Albums_Chart "UK Albums Chart"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2) number 8 on the [Canadian Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Albums_Chart "Canadian Albums Chart"),[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-CANstudio-3) and number 21 on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) Singles "[Crazy Train](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crazy_Train "Crazy Train")" and "[Mr Crowley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr_Crowley "Mr Crowley")" reached the top 50 of the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5) and the album has been certified four times platinum by the [Recording Industry Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_Association_of_America "Recording Industry Association of America") (RIAA).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-RIAA-6) 1981's _[Diary of a Madman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diary\_of\_a\_Madman\_(album) "Diary of a Madman (album)")_ reached the top 20 in the UK, Canada and the US,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-CANstudio-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) and was certified triple platinum by the RIAA.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-RIAA-6) The album was the last to feature Daisley and Kerslake, Osbourne of whom were fired from Black Sabbath and replaced by [Ronnie James Dio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronnie_James_Dio "Ronnie James Dio"), respectively, as well as the last to feature Rhoads, who died in a plane crash on 19 March 1982.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-allmusic-1)

Osbourne's first live album _[Speak of the Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_of\_the\_Devil\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Speak of the Devil (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_, featuring touring guitarist [Brad Gillis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brad_Gillis "Brad Gillis"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-7) reached number 21 in the UK and number 14 in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4)[Jake E. Lee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_E._Lee "Jake E. Lee") joined in 1983, with _[Bark at the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bark\_at\_the\_Moon "Bark at the Moon")_ released later in the year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-allmusic-1) The album reached number 24 in the UK and number 19 in the US,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) spawning UK top 40 singles "[Bark at the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bark_at_the_Moon_(song) "Bark at the Moon (song)")" and "[So Tired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So_Tired_(Ozzy_Osbourne_song) "So Tired (Ozzy Osbourne song)")".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5)_[The Ultimate Sin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ultimate\_Sin "The Ultimate Sin")_ followed in 1986, reaching the top ten in the UK and the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) Lead single "[Shot in the Dark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shot_in_the_Dark_(Ozzy_Osbourne_song) "Shot in the Dark (Ozzy Osbourne song)")" reached number 20 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") and number 68 on the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US100-8) The 1987 live album _[Tribute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribute\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Tribute (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_ charted in the top 20 in the UK and the top ten in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) After Lee was replaced by [Zakk Wylde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zakk_Wylde "Zakk Wylde"), _[No Rest for the Wicked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_Rest\_for\_the\_Wicked\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "No Rest for the Wicked (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_ was released in 1988 and reached number 23 in the UK and number 13 in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) The following year, Osbourne reached the top ten of the Hot 100 with [Lita Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lita_Ford "Lita Ford") on "[Close My Eyes Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_My_Eyes_Forever "Close My Eyes Forever")", peaking at number 8.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-USfeatured-9) 1991's _[No More Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_More\_Tears "No More Tears")_ reached the UK top 20,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2) the US top ten,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) and was certified four times platinum by the RIAA.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-RIAA-6) Singles "[No More Tears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_More_Tears_(Ozzy_Osbourne_song) "No More Tears (Ozzy Osbourne song)")" and "[Mama, I'm Coming Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mama,_I'm_Coming_Home "Mama, I'm Coming Home")" both reached the UK top 50 and charted on the _Billboard_ Hot 100.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US100-8) In 1992, Osbourne reached the UK Singles Chart top ten for the first time with [Was (Not Was)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Was_(Not_Was) "Was (Not Was)") and [Kim Basinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Basinger "Kim Basinger") on "[Shake Your Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shake_Your_Head "Shake Your Head")", which peaked at number 4.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKfeatured-10)

After briefly retiring,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-allmusic-1) Osbourne returned with _[Ozzmosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzmosis "Ozzmosis")_ in 1995, which was his first album to reach the top five of the _Billboard_ 200 when it peaked at number 4.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) Lead single "Perry Mason" reached number 23 on the UK Singles Chart.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5) 1997 compilation _[The Ozzman Cometh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ozzman\_Cometh "The Ozzman Cometh")_ reached the US top 20 and was certified double platinum.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-RIAA-6) In 2001 he released _[Down to Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down\_to\_Earth\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Down to Earth (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_, which reached number 19 in the UK and number 4 in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) The album spawned the successful single "[Dreamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamer_(Ozzy_Osbourne_song) "Dreamer (Ozzy Osbourne song)")", which was certified gold in Austria and Germany.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-IFPIAUT-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-BVMI-12) In 2003, Osbourne collaborated with daughter [Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Osbourne "Kelly Osbourne") on a recording of Black Sabbath's "[Changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changes_(Black_Sabbath_song) "Changes (Black Sabbath song)")", which was both artists' first (and to date, only) number-one single in the UK.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKsingles-5)_[The Essential Ozzy Osbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Essential\_Ozzy\_Osbourne "The Essential Ozzy Osbourne")_ was released the same year, reaching number 21 in the UK.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2) In 2005, Osbourne released an album of [cover versions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") entitled _[Under Cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under\_Cover\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Under Cover (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-13) which charted in the UK at number 67.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2) 2007's _[Black Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black\_Rain\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Black Rain (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_ reached number 8 in the UK and number 3 in the US, while 2010's _[Scream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scream\_(Ozzy\_Osbourne\_album) "Scream (Ozzy Osbourne album)")_ reached number 12 in the UK and number 4 in the US.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-US200-4) The compilation _[Memoirs Of A Madman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoirs\_of\_a\_Madman\_(album) "Memoirs of a Madman (album)")_ charted in the UK at number 23 in 2014.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-UKalbums-2)

As of 2014, Osbourne has sold more than 100 million albums worldwide, including those during his time in Black Sabbath.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozzy_Osbourne_discography#cite_note-15)

_**The Prisoner**_ is the seventh [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") album, recorded in 1969 and released in January 1970[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-5) for the [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") label, his final project for the label before moving to [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records"). It is dedicated to the memory of Dr. [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), who had been assassinated the previous year. Hancock suggested at the time that he had been able to get closer to his [real self](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_self "Real self") with this music than on any other previous album.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-notes-6) Participating musicians include tenor saxophonist [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), trumpeter [Johnny Coles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Coles "Johnny Coles") (on [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn")), trombonist [Garnett Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garnett_Brown "Garnett Brown"), flautist [Hubert Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Laws "Hubert Laws"), bassist [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams") and drummer [Albert “Tootie” Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tootie_Heath "Tootie Heath"). Hancock praised flute player Laws, suggesting that he was one of the finest flautists in classical or jazz music.

## Composition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Prisoner_(album)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Composition")]

Like his ambitious _[Speak Like a Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_Like\_a\_Child\_(album) "Speak Like a Child (album)")_, _The Prisoner_ purports to stand as a "social statement written in music". The title track seeks to express "how black people have been imprisoned for a long time." The piece was first heard live in 1968, during a performance at the University of California Jazz Festival. "Firewater" represents 'the social duality of the oppressor and the oppressed: the fire symbolises the heat in violence and (abuse of) power, whilst the feeling of water recalls Martin Luther King. "He Who Lives in Fear" also alludes to King, since he "had to live in an atmosphere charged with intimidation". Continuing the album's apparent theme, the "Promise of the Sun" symbolises "how the sun promises life and freedom to all living things, and yet blacks are not yet free."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-notes-6)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Prisoner_(album)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Reception")]

[Harvey Pekar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Pekar "Harvey Pekar"), writing for [DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat") in a contemporary review, awarded the album a perfect score and praised Hancock as "one of the most creative young jazzmen on the scene today".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-down_beat-2)

_**The Prisoner**_ is the seventh [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") album, recorded in 1969 and released in January 1970[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-5) for the [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") label, his final project for the label before moving to [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records"). It is dedicated to the memory of Dr. [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), who had been assassinated the previous year. Hancock suggested at the time that he had been able to get closer to his [real self](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_self "Real self") with this music than on any other previous album.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-notes-6) Participating musicians include tenor saxophonist [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), trumpeter [Johnny Coles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Coles "Johnny Coles") (on [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn")), trombonist [Garnett Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garnett_Brown "Garnett Brown"), flautist [Hubert Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Laws "Hubert Laws"), bassist [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams") and drummer [Albert “Tootie” Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tootie_Heath "Tootie Heath"). Hancock praised flute player Laws, suggesting that he was one of the finest flautists in classical or jazz music.

## Composition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Prisoner_(album)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Composition")]

Like his ambitious _[Speak Like a Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_Like\_a\_Child\_(album) "Speak Like a Child (album)")_, _The Prisoner_ purports to stand as a "social statement written in music". The title track seeks to express "how black people have been imprisoned for a long time." The piece was first heard live in 1968, during a performance at the University of California Jazz Festival. "Firewater" represents 'the social duality of the oppressor and the oppressed: the fire symbolises the heat in violence and (abuse of) power, whilst the feeling of water recalls Martin Luther King. "He Who Lives in Fear" also alludes to King, since he "had to live in an atmosphere charged with intimidation". Continuing the album's apparent theme, the "Promise of the Sun" symbolises "how the sun promises life and freedom to all living things, and yet blacks are not yet free."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-notes-6)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Prisoner_(album)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Reception")]

[Harvey Pekar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Pekar "Harvey Pekar"), writing for [DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat") in a contemporary review, awarded the album a perfect score and praised Hancock as "one of the most creative young jazzmen on the scene today".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-down_beat-2)

_**The Prisoner**_ is the seventh [Herbie Hancock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbie_Hancock "Herbie Hancock") album, recorded in 1969 and released in January 1970[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-5) for the [Blue Note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records") label, his final project for the label before moving to [Warner Bros. Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warner_Bros._Records "Warner Bros. Records"). It is dedicated to the memory of Dr. [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr."), who had been assassinated the previous year. Hancock suggested at the time that he had been able to get closer to his [real self](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_self "Real self") with this music than on any other previous album.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-notes-6) Participating musicians include tenor saxophonist [Joe Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Henderson "Joe Henderson"), trumpeter [Johnny Coles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Coles "Johnny Coles") (on [flugelhorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flugelhorn "Flugelhorn")), trombonist [Garnett Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garnett_Brown "Garnett Brown"), flautist [Hubert Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Laws "Hubert Laws"), bassist [Buster Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams") and drummer [Albert “Tootie” Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tootie_Heath "Tootie Heath"). Hancock praised flute player Laws, suggesting that he was one of the finest flautists in classical or jazz music.

## Composition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Prisoner_(album)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Composition")]

Like his ambitious _[Speak Like a Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speak\_Like\_a\_Child\_(album) "Speak Like a Child (album)")_, _The Prisoner_ purports to stand as a "social statement written in music". The title track seeks to express "how black people have been imprisoned for a long time." The piece was first heard live in 1968, during a performance at the University of California Jazz Festival. "Firewater" represents 'the social duality of the oppressor and the oppressed: the fire symbolises the heat in violence and (abuse of) power, whilst the feeling of water recalls Martin Luther King. "He Who Lives in Fear" also alludes to King, since he "had to live in an atmosphere charged with intimidation". Continuing the album's apparent theme, the "Promise of the Sun" symbolises "how the sun promises life and freedom to all living things, and yet blacks are not yet free."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-notes-6)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Prisoner_(album)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Reception")]

[Harvey Pekar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Pekar "Harvey Pekar"), writing for [DownBeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DownBeat "DownBeat") in a contemporary review, awarded the album a perfect score and praised Hancock as "one of the most creative young jazzmen on the scene today".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prisoner_(album)#cite_note-down_beat-2)

## Track listing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Prisoner_(album)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Track listing")]

All compositions by Herbie Hancock, except "Firewater" composed by [C. B. Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buster_Williams "Buster Williams").

**Side one**

1.   "I Have a Dream" – 10:58
2.   "The Prisoner" – 7:57

**Side two**

1.   "Firewater" – 7:33
2.   "He Who Lives in Fear" – 6:51
3.   "Promise of the Sun" – 7:52

**Bonus tracks on CD reissue**

2.   "The Prisoner" (alternate take) – 5:47
3.   "Firewater" (alternate take) – 8:38

*   April 21, 1969 – track 1

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Album Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_Art&redirect=no "Album Art"))

Design on an album's front cover

Not to be confused with [Cover album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album#Tribute_or_cover "Album").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Are_You_Experienced_-_US_cover-edit.jpg/250px-Are_You_Experienced_-_US_cover-edit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Are_You_Experienced_-_US_cover-edit.jpg)

The album cover for _[Are You Experienced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Are\_You\_Experienced "Are You Experienced")_ (1967) by the [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix") Experience

An **album cover** (also referred to as **album art**) is the front [packaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packaging "Packaging") art of a commercially released [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album "Album") or other audio recordings. The term can refer to:

*   the printed [paperboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paperboard "Paperboard") covers typically used to package: 
    *   sets of 10 in (25 cm) and 12 in (30 cm)[78 rpm records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/78_rpm_records "78 rpm records")
    *   singles and sets of 12 in (30 cm)[long-play records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record")
    *   sets of [45 rpm records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45_rpm_record "45 rpm record") (either in several connected sleeves or a box)

*   the front-facing panel of: 
    *   a [cassette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_tape "Cassette tape")[J-card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J-card "J-card")
    *   a [CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc "Compact disc")[package](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc_packaging "Optical disc packaging")

*   the primary image accompanying a [digital download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_download "Music download") of the album (or of its individual [tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_track "Music track")).

For all tangible records, the album art also serves as a part of the protective [sleeve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_sleeve "Record sleeve").

## Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early history")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Crosbyana.jpg/250px-Crosbyana.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crosbyana.jpg)

Cover for [Bing Crosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bing_Crosby "Bing Crosby")'s 1941 compilation album _[Crosbyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosbyana "Crosbyana")_ issued on six [78 records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/78_RPM "78 RPM")

Around 1909, 78 rpm records replaced the phonograph cylinder as the medium for recorded sound. The 78 rpm records were issued in both 11- and 12-inch-diameter sizes and were usually sold separately, in brown paper or cardboard sleeves that were sometimes plain and sometimes printed to show the producer or the retailer's name. These were invariably made out of [acidic paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acidic_paper "Acidic paper"), limiting conservability. Generally the sleeves had a circular cutout allowing the record label to be seen. Records could be laid on a shelf horizontally or stood upright on an edge, but because of their fragility, many broke in storage.

German record company [Odeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odeon_Records "Odeon Records") pioneered the "album" in 1909 when it released [the _Nutcracker Suite_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nutcracker "The Nutcracker") by [Tchaikovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Ilyich_Tchaikovsky "Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky") on four double-sided discs in a specially designed package.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-1) (It is not indicated what the specially designed package was.) The practice of issuing albums does not seem to have been taken up by other record companies for many years.

Beginning in the 1920s, bound collections of empty sleeves with a plain paperboard or leather cover were sold as "record albums" (similar to a photograph album) that customers could use to store their records. (The name "record album" was printed on some covers.) These empty albums were sold in both 10- and 12-inch sizes. The covers of these bound books were wider and taller than the records inside, allowing the record album to be placed on a shelf upright, like a book, and suspending the fragile records above the shelf, protecting them.

Starting in the 1930s, record companies began issuing collections of 78 rpm records by one performer or of one type of music in specially assembled collections. These albums of several 78 rpm records could include a collection of popular songs related by either performer or style, or extended-length [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), including complete [symphonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony "Symphony").

In 1938, [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") hired [Alex Steinweiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Steinweiss "Alex Steinweiss") as its first art director. He is credited with inventing the concept of album covers and cover art, replacing the plain covers used before. After his initial efforts at Columbia, other record companies followed his lead. By the late 1940s, record albums for all the major companies featured their own colorful paper covers in both 10- and 12-inch sizes. Some featured reproductions of classic art while others utilized original designs.

When the 10- and 12-inch long-playing records (LPs) came along in 1948, and box sets of 45 rpm records soon followed (see gramophone record), the name "album" was used for the new format of collections, and the creation of artistic original album covers continued.

## Formats

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formats")]

From the 1950s through to the 1980s, the 12-inch LP record and the 45 rpm record became the major formats for the distribution of [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music"). The LP format remains in use for new releases. The size of the typical cardboard LP sleeve cover is 12.375 in (31.43 cm) square.

Starting in the mid-1990s, the [compact disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc "Compact disc") (CD) was the most common form of physically distributed music products. [Packaging formats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc_packaging "Optical disc packaging") vary, including the jewel case (which since 1982 has been the most popular form of CD packaging), and the cardboard and plastic combination commonly known as a [Digipak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digipak "Digipak") (which has been a popular alternative form of packaging in recent years, but remains supplanted by the jewel case due to higher manufacturing costs and lower durability). Typically the album cover component of these packages is approximately 4.75 in (12.1 cm) square.

In the 1980s and early 1990s, CDs were often sold as jewel cases enclosed within cardboard [longboxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbox "Longbox") measuring 12 in (30 cm) by 6 in (15 cm), which provided more space for album artwork than the jewel cases they contained, but were seen as harmful to the environment since the cardboard box was typically discarded by the buyer soon after purchase. Major record labels in the United States stopped distributing CDs in longboxes as of April 1, 1993.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-2)

## Design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Design")]

See also: [Cover art §Album cover art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_art#Album_cover_art "Cover art")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/TheBeatles68LP.jpg/250px-TheBeatles68LP.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TheBeatles68LP.jpg)

The cover for _[The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Beatles\_(album) "The Beatles (album)")_, aka "The White Album", cited for its innovative design

Album covers are one of the various ways in which first impressions affect an audience's perception of a given musician or band, or other content of the album.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-3) Album covers' design cover may also add to how an audience forms an opinion of them and their music. There are various ways in which an album cover is visualized. Some examples include artists choosing to put a photo of themselves, which is one of the factors that add to the observation of the band, the musician, and the music.

The album cover eventually became an important part of the culture of music.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-Doggett_p_393-4) Under the influence of designers like [Bob Cato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Cato "Bob Cato"),[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] who at various stages in his long music career was vice president of creative services at both [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") and [United Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists "United Artists"), album covers became renowned for being a marketing tool and an expression of artistic intent.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-Doggett_p_393-4) Album art has also been discussed as an important postwar cultural expression.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-5)

During the early 1960s, [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' _[With the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/With\_the\_Beatles "With the Beatles")_, [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s _[The Times They Are a-Changin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times\_They\_Are\_a-Changin'\_(Bob\_Dylan\_album) "The Times They Are a-Changin' (Bob Dylan album)")_ and [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones")' [self-titled debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones_(album) "The Rolling Stones (album)") each contained a cover photograph designed to further the musical artist's public image. Author [Peter Doggett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Doggett "Peter Doggett") also highlights the cover of [Otis Redding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otis_Redding "Otis Redding")'s _[Otis Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otis\_Blue "Otis Blue")_, containing a photo of a young white woman, as a design that "played a dual role: she represented the transcendent power of the music, and obscured the race of its creator."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-Doggett_p_393-4) The standard portrait-based LP cover was further challenged over 1965–66 by Dylan's _[Bringing It All Back Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bringing\_It\_All\_Back\_Home "Bringing It All Back Home")_, through the inclusion of symbolic artefacts around the singer; the artificially stretched faces of the Beatles shown on their _[Rubber Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber\_Soul "Rubber Soul")_ album; and the darkened hues applied to the Rolling Stones on _[Aftermath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aftermath\_(The\_Rolling\_Stones\_album) "Aftermath (The Rolling Stones album)")_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-Doggett_p_393-4)

[Gatefold covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatefold "Gatefold") (a folded double cover) and inserts, often with lyric sheets, made the album cover a desirable work in its own right. Notable examples are the Beatles' _[Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt.\_Pepper's\_Lonely\_Hearts\_Club\_Band "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band")_, which had cut-out inserts, printed lyrics, and a gatefold sleeve, even though it was a single album; the Rolling Stones' _[Exile on Main Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exile\_on\_Main\_Street "Exile on Main Street")_, which had a gatefold and a series of 12 perforated postcards as inserts (taken by photographer [Norman Seeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Seeff "Norman Seeff")); and [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd")'s _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dark\_Side\_of\_the\_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_, which had a gatefold, lyrics, no title on the sleeve, and poster and sticker inserts. [The Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band "The Band")'s 1970 release _[Stage Fright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage\_Fright\_(album) "Stage Fright (album)")_, which included a photograph by Seeff as a poster insert, is an early example of LP artwork quickly becoming a collector's item. The move to the small (less than 1/4 the size of a record) CD format lost that impact, although attempts have been made to create a more desirable packaging for the CD format, for example the reissue of _Sgt. Pepper_, which had a cardboard box and booklet, or the use of oversized packaging.

The importance of design was such that some cover artists specialized or gained fame through their work. Such people include the design team [Hipgnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hipgnosis "Hipgnosis"), through their work on Pink Floyd albums and others; [Roger Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Dean_(artist) "Roger Dean (artist)"), famous for his [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") and [Greenslade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenslade "Greenslade") covers; [Cal Schenkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cal_Schenkel "Cal Schenkel"), for [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart")'s _[Trout Mask Replica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trout\_Mask\_Replica "Trout Mask Replica")_ and [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa")'s _[We're Only in It for the Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're\_Only\_in\_It\_for\_the\_Money "We're Only in It for the Money")_.

A genre of music that people have found issues in album covers is reggae. There are certain reggae artists that feel that the way they are displayed on their own album covers is not an accurate way of describing themselves and their culture. The stereotypical rasta lifestyle depicted on many reggae album covers is only displayed that way because this is what the white audience seemed to appreciate the most. This version of the reggae artists is what many people take notice of and what makes them unique in regards to other genres. However, these album covers do not accurately represent the core values of typical people in Jamaica but they deal with this representation because they know that the audience is familiar with the stereotypical rasta depiction. These album covers tend to display inauthentic versions of their considerations of style and sexuality and do not accurately display "Uptown" Jamaica.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-10)

## Packaging

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Packaging")]

The album cover is a component of the overall packaging of an album. These could be done in a single or a multiple ([gatefold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatefold "Gatefold")) sleeve. Especially in the case of vinyl records with paperboard sleeves, these packages are prone to wear and tear, although wear and tear does often take place to some degree on covers contained within plastic cases. A variety of treatments could be applied to improve both their appearance and durability, such as clear plastic wrap. Many products have been available for the storage of vinyl albums, often clear plastic sleeves.

The surface of a vinyl record is readily damaged, so aside from the outer [paperboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paperboard "Paperboard") sleeve, there is usually an inner protective cover to protect against dust and handling. This is normally shaped to allow it to readily slide within the outer cover. The inner sleeve is either thin white paper, either plain or printed with information on other recordings available from the same company, or a paper sleeve supporting a thin [plastic bag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_bag "Plastic bag"). These quite often have a circular cut out so that the record label can be read without directly handling the record, though when the inner sleeve is printed with lyrics, which became quite common, then there is usually no hole. Decca Records used a system of colour-coding on these sleeves where a blue color denoted a [stereophonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereophonic_sound "Stereophonic sound") recording while red denoted a [monophonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaural "Monaural") recording (the mono record players of the time were not always compatible with stereo records). This system was begun in the 1960s to reduce packaging costs.

[Packaging formats for compact discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc_packaging "Optical disc packaging") widened the variety of presentations as well, even as the size of the CD meant that album covers were no longer so large.

Besides the practicalities of identifying specific records, album covers serve the purpose of advertising the musical contents on the LP, through the use of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design"), [photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photography "Photography"), and/or [illustration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illustration "Illustration"). An album cover normally has the artist's name, sometimes in [logo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logo "Logo") form; and the album title. Occasionally, though more common on historical vinyl records, the cover may include a reference number; a branding (the [label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label")), and possibly a track listing. Other information is seldom included on the cover, and is usually contained on the rear or interior of the packaging, such as a track listing together with a more detailed list of those involved in making the record, band members, guest performers, engineers and producer. On the _spine_ of the package, the artist, title, and reference number are usually repeated so that albums can be identified while tightly packed on a shelf.

Parental advisory labels are warning labels that are required to be placed on album covers when the music on the album contains explicit content such as vulgar language. These labels have been known to be controversial when it comes to keeping underage audiences from this content. There are a few different theories on this, such as the "forbidden fruit" and "tainted fruit" theories. The "forbidden fruit" theory states that when a child sees the parental advisory label on an album cover they will be more likely to listen to it because there is an increased attractiveness to the music. There are many adolescents that follow the "forbidden fruit" theory as a way to either lash out at their parents or to make themselves feel more mature than they are. They may use explicit music as a way to be rebellious and to appear cooler to their friends, even if they are much too young to be exposed to that kind of music. The "tainted fruit" theory states that the child will see the label and immediately know to avoid this kind of content because it is inappropriate for their age. These children are the ones who see the label and do not even acknowledge this album or these songs because they know that it is not made for them. The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) introduced this warning label and it is now a requirement on any explicit music. However, the RIAA is unable to actually control whether or not adolescents will be listening to the music but as of now there is no way to fully control what these children are doing. ## Album covers in the age of downloads and streaming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Album covers in the age of downloads and streaming")]

In August 2008, album cover designer [Peter Saville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Saville_(artist) "Peter Saville (artist)") suggested that the album cover was dead.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-13) Album art is still considered a vital part of the listening experience to many.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-14)

MP3, WMA, and M4A ([Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") format) music files can contain embedded digital album artworks (called cover images or simply covers) in jpeg format.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-15) One digital solution is the [iTunes LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_LP "ITunes LP") format for interactive album artwork introduced by Apple in 2009. Resolution for digital album covers should be at least 800×800 (1:1 aspect ratio); lower resolutions might not look good on newer devices.

Some artists have used Internet technology to generate even more cover art. For instance, [Nine Inch Nails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Inch_Nails "Nine Inch Nails") initially released its album _[The Slip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Slip\_(album) "The Slip (album)")_ as a free download on the band's website, attaching separate but thematically connected images to each individual track.

## Controversial covers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Controversial covers")]

See also: [List of controversial album art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_controversial_album_art "List of controversial album art")

Some album covers have been banned due to depicting violence, nudity, religious or other offensive imagery. For instance, [Guns N' Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guns_N'_Roses "Guns N' Roses")'s 1987 album _[Appetite for Destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appetite\_for\_Destruction "Appetite for Destruction")_'s original cover depicted a robot rapist about to be punished by a metal avenger, and [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West")'s 2010 album _[My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Beautiful\_Dark\_Twisted\_Fantasy "My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy")_ depicted West naked and being straddled by a [phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_(mythology) "Phoenix (mythology)") with her bare breasts and buttocks showing. Other covers were controversial due to [infringement of intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property_infringement "Intellectual property infringement") or [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_infringement "Copyright infringement").
