From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [Album Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_Art&redirect=no "Album Art"))

Design on an album's front cover

Not to be confused with [Cover album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album#Tribute_or_cover "Album").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Are_You_Experienced_-_US_cover-edit.jpg/250px-Are_You_Experienced_-_US_cover-edit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Are_You_Experienced_-_US_cover-edit.jpg)

The album cover for _[Are You Experienced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Are\_You\_Experienced "Are You Experienced")_ (1967) by the [Jimi Hendrix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimi_Hendrix "Jimi Hendrix") Experience

An **album cover** (also referred to as **album art**) is the front [packaging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Packaging "Packaging") art of a commercially released [studio album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album "Album") or other audio recordings. The term can refer to:

*   the printed [paperboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paperboard "Paperboard") covers typically used to package: 
    *   sets of 10 in (25 cm) and 12 in (30 cm)[78 rpm records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/78_rpm_records "78 rpm records")
    *   singles and sets of 12 in (30 cm)[long-play records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record")
    *   sets of [45 rpm records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/45_rpm_record "45 rpm record") (either in several connected sleeves or a box)

*   the front-facing panel of: 
    *   a [cassette](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassette_tape "Cassette tape")[J-card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J-card "J-card")
    *   a [CD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc "Compact disc")[package](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc_packaging "Optical disc packaging")

*   the primary image accompanying a [digital download](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_download "Music download") of the album (or of its individual [tracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_track "Music track")).

For all tangible records, the album art also serves as a part of the protective [sleeve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_sleeve "Record sleeve").

## Early history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early history")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Crosbyana.jpg/250px-Crosbyana.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Crosbyana.jpg)

Cover for [Bing Crosby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bing_Crosby "Bing Crosby")'s 1941 compilation album _[Crosbyana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crosbyana "Crosbyana")_ issued on six [78 records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/78_RPM "78 RPM")

Around 1909, 78 rpm records replaced the phonograph cylinder as the medium for recorded sound. The 78 rpm records were issued in both 11- and 12-inch-diameter sizes and were usually sold separately, in brown paper or cardboard sleeves that were sometimes plain and sometimes printed to show the producer or the retailer's name. These were invariably made out of [acidic paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acidic_paper "Acidic paper"), limiting conservability. Generally the sleeves had a circular cutout allowing the record label to be seen. Records could be laid on a shelf horizontally or stood upright on an edge, but because of their fragility, many broke in storage.

German record company [Odeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odeon_Records "Odeon Records") pioneered the "album" in 1909 when it released [the _Nutcracker Suite_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Nutcracker "The Nutcracker") by [Tchaikovsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyotr_Ilyich_Tchaikovsky "Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky") on four double-sided discs in a specially designed package.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-1) (It is not indicated what the specially designed package was.) The practice of issuing albums does not seem to have been taken up by other record companies for many years.

Beginning in the 1920s, bound collections of empty sleeves with a plain paperboard or leather cover were sold as "record albums" (similar to a photograph album) that customers could use to store their records. (The name "record album" was printed on some covers.) These empty albums were sold in both 10- and 12-inch sizes. The covers of these bound books were wider and taller than the records inside, allowing the record album to be placed on a shelf upright, like a book, and suspending the fragile records above the shelf, protecting them.

Starting in the 1930s, record companies began issuing collections of 78 rpm records by one performer or of one type of music in specially assembled collections. These albums of several 78 rpm records could include a collection of popular songs related by either performer or style, or extended-length [classical music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), including complete [symphonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony "Symphony").

In 1938, [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") hired [Alex Steinweiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Steinweiss "Alex Steinweiss") as its first art director. He is credited with inventing the concept of album covers and cover art, replacing the plain covers used before. After his initial efforts at Columbia, other record companies followed his lead. By the late 1940s, record albums for all the major companies featured their own colorful paper covers in both 10- and 12-inch sizes. Some featured reproductions of classic art while others utilized original designs.

When the 10- and 12-inch long-playing records (LPs) came along in 1948, and box sets of 45 rpm records soon followed (see gramophone record), the name "album" was used for the new format of collections, and the creation of artistic original album covers continued.

## Formats

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formats")]

From the 1950s through to the 1980s, the 12-inch LP record and the 45 rpm record became the major formats for the distribution of [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music"). The LP format remains in use for new releases. The size of the typical cardboard LP sleeve cover is 12.375 in (31.43 cm) square.

Starting in the mid-1990s, the [compact disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compact_disc "Compact disc") (CD) was the most common form of physically distributed music products. [Packaging formats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc_packaging "Optical disc packaging") vary, including the jewel case (which since 1982 has been the most popular form of CD packaging), and the cardboard and plastic combination commonly known as a [Digipak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digipak "Digipak") (which has been a popular alternative form of packaging in recent years, but remains supplanted by the jewel case due to higher manufacturing costs and lower durability). Typically the album cover component of these packages is approximately 4.75 in (12.1 cm) square.

In the 1980s and early 1990s, CDs were often sold as jewel cases enclosed within cardboard [longboxes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longbox "Longbox") measuring 12 in (30 cm) by 6 in (15 cm), which provided more space for album artwork than the jewel cases they contained, but were seen as harmful to the environment since the cardboard box was typically discarded by the buyer soon after purchase. Major record labels in the United States stopped distributing CDs in longboxes as of April 1, 1993.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-2)

## Design

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Design")]

See also: [Cover art §Album cover art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_art#Album_cover_art "Cover art")

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/TheBeatles68LP.jpg/250px-TheBeatles68LP.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TheBeatles68LP.jpg)

The cover for _[The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Beatles\_(album) "The Beatles (album)")_, aka "The White Album", cited for its innovative design

Album covers are one of the various ways in which first impressions affect an audience's perception of a given musician or band, or other content of the album.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-3) Album covers' design cover may also add to how an audience forms an opinion of them and their music. There are various ways in which an album cover is visualized. Some examples include artists choosing to put a photo of themselves, which is one of the factors that add to the observation of the band, the musician, and the music.

The album cover eventually became an important part of the culture of music.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-Doggett_p_393-4) Under the influence of designers like [Bob Cato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Cato "Bob Cato"),[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] who at various stages in his long music career was vice president of creative services at both [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records") and [United Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists "United Artists"), album covers became renowned for being a marketing tool and an expression of artistic intent.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-Doggett_p_393-4) Album art has also been discussed as an important postwar cultural expression.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-5)

During the early 1960s, [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' _[With the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/With\_the\_Beatles "With the Beatles")_, [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")'s _[The Times They Are a-Changin'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times\_They\_Are\_a-Changin'\_(Bob\_Dylan\_album) "The Times They Are a-Changin' (Bob Dylan album)")_ and [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones")' [self-titled debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones_(album) "The Rolling Stones (album)") each contained a cover photograph designed to further the musical artist's public image. Author [Peter Doggett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Doggett "Peter Doggett") also highlights the cover of [Otis Redding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otis_Redding "Otis Redding")'s _[Otis Blue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otis\_Blue "Otis Blue")_, containing a photo of a young white woman, as a design that "played a dual role: she represented the transcendent power of the music, and obscured the race of its creator."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-Doggett_p_393-4) The standard portrait-based LP cover was further challenged over 1965–66 by Dylan's _[Bringing It All Back Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bringing\_It\_All\_Back\_Home "Bringing It All Back Home")_, through the inclusion of symbolic artefacts around the singer; the artificially stretched faces of the Beatles shown on their _[Rubber Soul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubber\_Soul "Rubber Soul")_ album; and the darkened hues applied to the Rolling Stones on _[Aftermath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aftermath\_(The\_Rolling\_Stones\_album) "Aftermath (The Rolling Stones album)")_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-Doggett_p_393-4)

[Gatefold covers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatefold "Gatefold") (a folded double cover) and inserts, often with lyric sheets, made the album cover a desirable work in its own right. Notable examples are the Beatles' _[Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sgt.\_Pepper's\_Lonely\_Hearts\_Club\_Band "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band")_, which had cut-out inserts, printed lyrics, and a gatefold sleeve, even though it was a single album; the Rolling Stones' _[Exile on Main Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exile\_on\_Main\_Street "Exile on Main Street")_, which had a gatefold and a series of 12 perforated postcards as inserts (taken by photographer [Norman Seeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Seeff "Norman Seeff")); and [Pink Floyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pink_Floyd "Pink Floyd")'s _[The Dark Side of the Moon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dark\_Side\_of\_the\_Moon "The Dark Side of the Moon")_, which had a gatefold, lyrics, no title on the sleeve, and poster and sticker inserts. [The Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band "The Band")'s 1970 release _[Stage Fright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage\_Fright\_(album) "Stage Fright (album)")_, which included a photograph by Seeff as a poster insert, is an early example of LP artwork quickly becoming a collector's item. The move to the small (less than 1/4 the size of a record) CD format lost that impact, although attempts have been made to create a more desirable packaging for the CD format, for example the reissue of _Sgt. Pepper_, which had a cardboard box and booklet, or the use of oversized packaging.

The importance of design was such that some cover artists specialized or gained fame through their work. Such people include the design team [Hipgnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hipgnosis "Hipgnosis"), through their work on Pink Floyd albums and others; [Roger Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Dean_(artist) "Roger Dean (artist)"), famous for his [Yes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yes_(band) "Yes (band)") and [Greenslade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenslade "Greenslade") covers; [Cal Schenkel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cal_Schenkel "Cal Schenkel"), for [Captain Beefheart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Captain_Beefheart "Captain Beefheart")'s _[Trout Mask Replica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trout\_Mask\_Replica "Trout Mask Replica")_ and [Frank Zappa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Zappa "Frank Zappa")'s _[We're Only in It for the Money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're\_Only\_in\_It\_for\_the\_Money "We're Only in It for the Money")_.

The talents of many photographers and illustrators, inside and outside of the music industry have been used to produce a numerous amount of LP/CD covers. Photographer [Mick Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Rock "Mick Rock") produced many notable album covers of the 1970s, including [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_(band) "Queen (band)")'s _[Queen II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen\_II "Queen II")_ (recreated for their classic music video "[Bohemian Rhapsody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohemian_Rhapsody "Bohemian Rhapsody")"), [Syd Barrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syd_Barrett "Syd Barrett")'s _[The Madcap Laughs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Madcap\_Laughs "The Madcap Laughs")_, and [Lou Reed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Reed "Lou Reed")'s _[Transformer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transformer\_(Lou\_Reed\_album) "Transformer (Lou Reed album)")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-6) From 1972 to 1975, photographer [Norman Seeff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Seeff "Norman Seeff") was creative director at [United Artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Artists "United Artists") and in addition to his many cover photographs ([The Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band "The Band"), [Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_(band) "Kiss (band)")'s _[Hotter than Hell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hotter\_than\_Hell\_(album) "Hotter than Hell (album)")_, [Joni Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joni_Mitchell "Joni Mitchell")'s _[Hejira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hejira\_(album) "Hejira (album)")_, etc.), he art directed dozens of album covers including _[Exile on Main Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exile\_on\_Main\_St. "Exile on Main St.")_, many of which received [Grammy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") nominations. A genre of music that people have found issues in album covers is reggae. There are certain reggae artists that feel that the way they are displayed on their own album covers is not an accurate way of describing themselves and their culture. The stereotypical rasta lifestyle depicted on many reggae album covers is only displayed that way because this is what the white audience seemed to appreciate the most. This version of the reggae artists is what many people take notice of and what makes them unique in regards to other genres. However, these album covers do not accurately represent the core values of typical people in Jamaica but they deal with this representation because they know that the audience is familiar with the stereotypical rasta depiction. These album covers tend to display inauthentic versions of their considerations of style and sexuality and do not accurately display "Uptown" Jamaica.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-10)

Album cover art was the subject of a 2011 documentary film, _The Cover Story: Album Art_, by Eric Christensen, a [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area") record collector.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-11)

The physical design of album covers has been the subject of creative innovation. _[Ogden's Nut Gone Flake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ogden's\_Nut\_Gone\_Flake "Ogden's Nut Gone Flake")_ by the [Small Faces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_Faces "Small Faces") was originally in a circular metal tin, and _[Happy to Meet – Sorry to Part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy\_to\_Meet\_%E2%80%93\_Sorry\_to\_Part "Happy to Meet – Sorry to Part")_ by [Horslips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horslips "Horslips") was in an octagonal package. [_Anyway_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyway_(Family_album) "Anyway (Family album)") by [Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Family_(British_band) "Family (British band)") was originally issued in an opaque plastic package through which a design (a Leonardo sketch) could be seen. _[Magical Mystery Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magical\_Mystery\_Tour\_(album) "Magical Mystery Tour (album)")_ by the Beatles was first released as a double [EP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") with a booklet between the records. _Sgt. Pepper_ contained a cardboard sheet of images, and _[The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Beatles\_(album) "The Beatles (album)")_ (often referred to as the White Album) contained four large glossy photos of the individual Beatles along with a poster-sized collage. _[Live at Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_at\_Leeds "Live at Leeds")_ by [The Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who") also contained a generous supply of posters and printed material. _[Led Zeppelin III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led\_Zeppelin\_III "Led Zeppelin III")_ had a front cover that contained a revolving disc which brought different images into view through small cut-outs in the outer sleeve. A similar effect was used for the band's later album _[Physical Graffiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical\_Graffiti "Physical Graffiti")_ with cut-outs of the windows of a brownstone building. The original issue of _[Sticky Fingers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sticky\_Fingers "Sticky Fingers")_ by the Rolling Stones had an actual zipper incorporated into the picture of the crotch area of a pair of jeans. _[The Velvet Underground and Nico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Velvet\_Underground\_and\_Nico "The Velvet Underground and Nico")_ album had a Warhol-designed cardboard banana on the cover that could be peeled back. The record company [Vertigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertigo_Records "Vertigo Records") had a black-and-white design on the centre label that produced a hypnotic optical effect when the disc revolved on the turntable.

## Packaging

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Packaging")]

The album cover is a component of the overall packaging of an album. These could be done in a single or a multiple ([gatefold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gatefold "Gatefold")) sleeve. Especially in the case of vinyl records with paperboard sleeves, these packages are prone to wear and tear, although wear and tear does often take place to some degree on covers contained within plastic cases. A variety of treatments could be applied to improve both their appearance and durability, such as clear plastic wrap. Many products have been available for the storage of vinyl albums, often clear plastic sleeves.

The surface of a vinyl record is readily damaged, so aside from the outer [paperboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paperboard "Paperboard") sleeve, there is usually an inner protective cover to protect against dust and handling. This is normally shaped to allow it to readily slide within the outer cover. The inner sleeve is either thin white paper, either plain or printed with information on other recordings available from the same company, or a paper sleeve supporting a thin [plastic bag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plastic_bag "Plastic bag"). These quite often have a circular cut out so that the record label can be read without directly handling the record, though when the inner sleeve is printed with lyrics, which became quite common, then there is usually no hole. Decca Records used a system of colour-coding on these sleeves where a blue color denoted a [stereophonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereophonic_sound "Stereophonic sound") recording while red denoted a [monophonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaural "Monaural") recording (the mono record players of the time were not always compatible with stereo records). This system was begun in the 1960s to reduce packaging costs.

[Packaging formats for compact discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_disc_packaging "Optical disc packaging") widened the variety of presentations as well, even as the size of the CD meant that album covers were no longer so large.

Besides the practicalities of identifying specific records, album covers serve the purpose of advertising the musical contents on the LP, through the use of [graphic design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphic_design "Graphic design"), [photography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photography "Photography"), and/or [illustration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illustration "Illustration"). An album cover normally has the artist's name, sometimes in [logo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logo "Logo") form; and the album title. Occasionally, though more common on historical vinyl records, the cover may include a reference number; a branding (the [label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_label "Record label")), and possibly a track listing. Other information is seldom included on the cover, and is usually contained on the rear or interior of the packaging, such as a track listing together with a more detailed list of those involved in making the record, band members, guest performers, engineers and producer. On the _spine_ of the package, the artist, title, and reference number are usually repeated so that albums can be identified while tightly packed on a shelf.

Parental advisory labels are warning labels that are required to be placed on album covers when the music on the album contains explicit content such as vulgar language. These labels have been known to be controversial when it comes to keeping underage audiences from this content. There are a few different theories on this, such as the "forbidden fruit" and "tainted fruit" theories. The "forbidden fruit" theory states that when a child sees the parental advisory label on an album cover they will be more likely to listen to it because there is an increased attractiveness to the music. There are many adolescents that follow the "forbidden fruit" theory as a way to either lash out at their parents or to make themselves feel more mature than they are. They may use explicit music as a way to be rebellious and to appear cooler to their friends, even if they are much too young to be exposed to that kind of music. The "tainted fruit" theory states that the child will see the label and immediately know to avoid this kind of content because it is inappropriate for their age. These children are the ones who see the label and do not even acknowledge this album or these songs because they know that it is not made for them. The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) introduced this warning label and it is now a requirement on any explicit music. However, the RIAA is unable to actually control whether or not adolescents will be listening to the music but as of now there is no way to fully control what these children are doing. [[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-12)

## Album covers in the age of downloads and streaming

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Album covers in the age of downloads and streaming")]

In August 2008, album cover designer [Peter Saville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Saville_(artist) "Peter Saville (artist)") suggested that the album cover was dead.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-13) Album art is still considered a vital part of the listening experience to many.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-14)

MP3, WMA, and M4A ([Apple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") format) music files can contain embedded digital album artworks (called cover images or simply covers) in jpeg format.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_Art#cite_note-15) One digital solution is the [iTunes LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_LP "ITunes LP") format for interactive album artwork introduced by Apple in 2009. Resolution for digital album covers should be at least 800×800 (1:1 aspect ratio); lower resolutions might not look good on newer devices.

Some artists have used Internet technology to generate even more cover art. For instance, [Nine Inch Nails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Inch_Nails "Nine Inch Nails") initially released its album _[The Slip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Slip\_(album) "The Slip (album)")_ as a free download on the band's website, attaching separate but thematically connected images to each individual track.

## Controversial covers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Album_cover&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Controversial covers")]

See also: [List of controversial album art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_controversial_album_art "List of controversial album art")

Some album covers have been banned due to depicting violence, nudity, religious or other offensive imagery. For instance, [Guns N' Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guns_N'_Roses "Guns N' Roses")'s 1987 album _[Appetite for Destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appetite\_for\_Destruction "Appetite for Destruction")_'s original cover depicted a robot rapist about to be punished by a metal avenger, and [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West")'s 2010 album _[My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Beautiful\_Dark\_Twisted\_Fantasy "My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy")_ depicted West naked and being straddled by a [phoenix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_(mythology) "Phoenix (mythology)") with her bare breasts and buttocks showing. Other covers were controversial due to [infringement of intellectual property](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intellectual_property_infringement "Intellectual property infringement") or [copyright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copyright_infringement "Copyright infringement").

The**Ramones**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-1) were an American [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") band formed in the New York City neighborhood [Forest Hills, Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Hills,_Queens "Forest Hills, Queens"), in 1974. Known for helping establish the punk movement in the United States and elsewhere, the Ramones are often recognized as one of the first bands of the genre. Although they never achieved significant commercial success during their existence, the band is highly influential in [punk culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_subculture "Punk subculture").

All members adopted pseudonyms ending with the surname Ramone, although none were biologically related; they were inspired by [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney"), who used the stage name Paul Ramon when [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles") were still calling themselves The Silver Beetles. The Ramones performed 2,263 concerts, touring virtually nonstop for 22 years,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-HallofFame-2) and released fourteen studio albums. In 1996, after a tour as part of the [Lollapalooza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lollapalooza "Lollapalooza") music festival, they played a [farewell concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're_Outta_Here! "We're Outta Here!") in Los Angeles and disbanded.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Schinder559-3)

By 2014, all four original members had died: lead singer [Joey Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Ramone "Joey Ramone") (1951–2001), bassist [Dee Dee Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dee_Dee_Ramone "Dee Dee Ramone") (1951–2002), guitarist [Johnny Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Ramone "Johnny Ramone") (1948–2004) and drummer [Tommy Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Ramone "Tommy Ramone") (1949–2014).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-AP-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-nytimes-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Sisario-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-guardian-7) The Ramones had experienced a few lineup changes, with Joey and Johnny as the only constant members. Tommy left the band in 1978 to pursue a career in [record production](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Record_producer "Record producer"), and was replaced by [Marky Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marky_Ramone "Marky Ramone"), who himself was replaced by [Richie Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richie_Ramone "Richie Ramone") in 1983. Following Richie's departure in 1987, and a brief stint with [Elvis Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clem_Burke "Clem Burke"), Marky rejoined the band and Dee Dee left two years later, being replaced by [C. J. Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._J._Ramone "C. J. Ramone"). From 1989 to their breakup in 1996, the Ramones consisted of Joey, Johnny, Marky and C. J. Ramone.

Recognition of the band's importance has built over the years.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-8) The Ramones were ranked number 26 in _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ magazine's 2004 list of the "[100 Greatest Artists of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_100_Greatest_Artists_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 100 Greatest Artists of All Time")"[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-9) and number 17 in [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1")'s 2012 television series _100 Greatest Artists of Hard Rock_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-10) In 2002, the Ramones were ranked the second-greatest band of all time by _[Spin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spin\_(magazine) "Spin (magazine)")_, trailing only [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-11) On March 18, 2002, the original four members and Tommy's replacement on drums, Marky Ramone, were all inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") in their first year of eligibility.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-HallofFame-2)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-12) In 2011, the band was awarded a [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Sterndan-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-grammy1-14)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Formation (1974–1975)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formation (1974–1975)")]

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d6/ForestHillsHS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ForestHillsHS.jpg)

[Forest Hills High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Hills_High_School_(New_York) "Forest Hills High School (New York)"), attended by the four original members of the Ramones

The original members of the band met in and around the middle-class neighborhood of [Forest Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Hills,_Queens "Forest Hills, Queens") in the New York City borough of [Queens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queens "Queens"). [John Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Ramone "Johnny Ramone") and [Thomas Erdelyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Ramone "Tommy Ramone") had both been in a high-school [garage band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garage_rock "Garage rock") from 1965 to 1967 known as the Tangerine Puppets.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-15) They became friends with [Douglas Colvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dee_Dee_Ramone "Dee Dee Ramone"), who had recently moved to the area from Germany,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-eotc-16) and [Jeff Hyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Ramone "Joey Ramone"), who was the singer for the [glam rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glam_rock "Glam rock") band [Sniper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sniper_(American_band) "Sniper (American band)"), founded in 1972.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Time-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-19)

The Ramones began taking shape in early 1974 when Cummings and Colvin invited Hyman to join them in a band. Colvin wanted to play guitar and sing, Cummings would also play guitar and Hyman would play drums. The lineup was to be completed with their friend Richie Stern on bass. However, after only a few rehearsals it became clear that Stern could not play bass, so the group parted ways with him and became a trio, with Colvin switching from guitar to bass in addition to singing while Cummings became the only guitarist.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Commando-20) Colvin was the first to adopt the name "Ramone", calling himself Dee Dee Ramone. He was inspired by [Paul McCartney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_McCartney "Paul McCartney")'s use of the pseudonym Paul Ramon during his [Silver Beetles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles#The_Quarrymen_and_name_changes "The Beatles") days.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-MM32-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-22) Dee Dee convinced the other members to take on the name and came up with the idea of calling the band the Ramones.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-punkbands-23) Hyman and Cummings became Joey and Johnny Ramone, respectively.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-punkbands-23)

A friend of the band, Monte A. Melnick (later their tour manager), helped to arrange rehearsal time for them at Manhattan's Performance Studios, where he worked. Johnny's former bandmate Erdelyi was set to become their manager. Soon after the band was formed, Dee Dee realized that he could not sing and play his bass guitar simultaneously; with Erdelyi's encouragement, Joey became the band's new lead singer.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-MM32-21) Dee Dee would continue, however, to count off each song's tempo with his signature rapid-fire shout of "1-2-3-4!" Joey soon similarly realized that he could not sing and play drums simultaneously and left the position of drummer. While auditioning prospective replacements, Erdelyi would often take to the drums and demonstrate how to play the songs. It became apparent that he was able to perform the group's music better than anyone else, and he joined the band as Tommy Ramone.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-MM33-24)

The Ramones played before an audience for the first time on March 30, 1974, at Performance Studios.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-HallofFame-2) The songs they played were very fast and very short; most clocked in at under two minutes. Around this time, a new music scene was emerging in New York centered on two clubs in [downtown Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Manhattan "Lower Manhattan")—[Max's Kansas City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max's_Kansas_City "Max's Kansas City") and, more famously, [CBGB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBGB "CBGB") (usually referred to as CBGB's). The Ramones made their CBGB debut on August 16, 1974.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-25)[Legs McNeil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legs_McNeil "Legs McNeil"), who cofounded _[Punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk\_(magazine) "Punk (magazine)")_ magazine the following year, later described the impact of that performance: "They were all wearing these black leather jackets. And they counted off this song ... and it was just this wall of noise ... They looked so striking. These guys were not hippies. This was something completely new."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-26)

The band swiftly became regulars at the club, playing there seventy-four times by the end of the year. After garnering considerable attention for their performances—which averaged about seventeen minutes from beginning to end—the group was signed to a recording contract in late 1975 by [Seymour Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seymour_Stein "Seymour Stein") of [Sire Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sire_Records "Sire Records"). Sire [A&R](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artists_and_repertoire "Artists and repertoire") man [Craig Leon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Leon "Craig Leon")[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-MM101-27) saw the band and brought them to the attention of the label. Stein's wife, [Linda Stein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_S._Stein "Linda S. Stein"), saw the band play at Mothers; she would later co-manage them along with [Danny Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Fields "Danny Fields").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Bessman,_211-28) By this time, the Ramones were recognized as leaders of the new scene that was increasingly being referred to as "[punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock")".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-St62-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-30) The group's unusual frontman had a lot to do with their impact. As Dee Dee explained, "All the other singers [in New York] were copying [David Johansen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Johansen "David Johansen") [of the [New York Dolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Dolls "New York Dolls")], who was copying [Mick Jagger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mick_Jagger "Mick Jagger") ... But Joey was unique, totally unique."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-31)

### Spearheading punk (1976–1977)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Spearheading punk (1976–1977)")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Ramones_Toronto_1976.jpg/250px-Ramones_Toronto_1976.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ramones_Toronto_1976.jpg)

Ramones performing in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto,_Canada "Toronto, Canada") in 1976

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/2e/PunkMagazine.jpg/250px-PunkMagazine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:PunkMagazine.jpg)

April 1976 issue of _[Punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk\_(magazine) "Punk (magazine)")_. The cover image of Joey, by _Punk_ cofounder [John Holmstrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Holmstrom "John Holmstrom"), was inspired by the work of comic artist [Will Eisner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Will_Eisner "Will Eisner").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Shirley-32) Holmstrom would go on to do album art for _[Rocket to Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket\_to\_Russia "Rocket to Russia")_ and _[Road to Ruin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road\_to\_Ruin\_(Ramones\_album) "Road to Ruin (Ramones album)")_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-33)

The Ramones recorded their debut album, _[Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones\_(album) "Ramones (album)")_, in February 1976. Of the fourteen songs on the album, the longest, "I Don't Wanna Go Down to the Basement", barely surpassed two and a half minutes. While the songwriting credits were shared by the entire band, and each member did contribute some writing, much of the writing was done by Dee Dee.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-34)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-35) The _Ramones_ album was produced by Sire's [Craig Leon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Leon "Craig Leon"), with Tommy as associate producer, on an extremely low budget of about $6,400 and released on April 23.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-36)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-37) The now-iconic front cover photograph of the band was taken by Roberta Bayley, a photographer for _[Punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk\_(magazine) "Punk (magazine)")_ magazine.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-38)_Punk_, which was largely responsible for codifying the term for the scene emerging around CBGB, ran a cover story on the Ramones in its third issue, the same month as the album's release.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Shirley-32)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-39)

The Ramones' debut album was greeted by rock critics with glowing reviews. _[The Village Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Village\_Voice "The Village Voice")_'s [Robert Christgau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Christgau "Robert Christgau") wrote, "I love this record—love it—even though I know these boys flirt with images of brutality (Nazi especially) ... For me, it blows everything else off the radio."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-40) In _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_, [Paul Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Nelson_(critic) "Paul Nelson (critic)") described it as "constructed almost entirely of rhythm tracks of an exhilarating intensity rock & roll has not experienced since its earliest days." Characterizing the band as "authentic American primitives whose work has to be heard to be understood", he declared, "It is time popular music followed the other arts in honoring its primitives."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-41)_[Newsday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsday "Newsday")_'s Wayne Robbins simply anointed the Ramones as "the best young rock 'n' roll band in the known universe."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-42)

Despite Sire's high hopes for it,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-43)_Ramones_ was not a commercial success, reaching only number 111 on the _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard\_charts "Billboard charts")_ album chart.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-44) The two singles issued from the album, "[Blitzkrieg Bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blitzkrieg_Bop "Blitzkrieg Bop")" and "I Wanna Be Your Boyfriend", failed to chart. At the band's first major performance outside of New York, a June date in [Youngstown, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youngstown,_Ohio "Youngstown, Ohio"), members of Cleveland punk legends Frankenstein aka the [Dead Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dead_Boys "The Dead Boys") were present and struck up a friendship with the band.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-45) It was not until they made a brief tour of England that they began to see the fruits of their labor; a performance at the [Roundhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundhouse_(venue) "Roundhouse (venue)") in London on July 4, 1976, with [The Stranglers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stranglers "The Stranglers") supporting the [Flamin' Groovies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamin'_Groovies "Flamin' Groovies"), organized by Linda Stein, was a resounding success.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-46)[T. Rex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._Rex_(band) "T. Rex (band)") leader [Marc Bolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Bolan "Marc Bolan") was in attendance at the Roundhouse show and was invited on stage.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-48) Their Roundhouse appearance and a club date the following night—where the band met members of the [Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols") and [the Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clash "The Clash")—helped galvanize the burgeoning UK punk rock scene.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-AP-4) The Flamin' Groovies/Ramones double bill was successfully reprised at the [Roxy Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roxy_Theatre_(West_Hollywood) "Roxy Theatre (West Hollywood)") in Los Angeles the following month, fueling the [punk scene there](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock_in_California "Punk rock in California") as well. The Ramones were becoming an increasingly popular live act—a Toronto performance in September energized yet another growing punk scene.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-LW-49)

Their next two albums, _[Leave Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leave\_Home "Leave Home")_ and _[Rocket to Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocket\_to\_Russia "Rocket to Russia")_, were both released in 1977, and produced by Tommy and [Tony Bongiovi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Bongiovi "Tony Bongiovi"), the second cousin of [Jon Bon Jovi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Bon_Jovi "Jon Bon Jovi").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-50)_Leave Home_ met with even less chart success than _Ramones_, though it did include "Pinhead", which became one of the band's signature songs with its chanted refrain of "Gabba gabba hey!" _Leave Home_ also included a fast-paced cover of the oldie "[California Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Sun "California Sun")", written by Henry Glover & Morris Levy, and originally recorded by Joe Jones,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-51) though the Ramones based their version on the remake by the Rivieras. _Rocket to Russia_ was the band's highest-charting album to date, reaching number 49 on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-52) In _Rolling Stone_, critic [Dave Marsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Marsh "Dave Marsh") called it "the best American rock & roll of the year".[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-53) The album also featured the first Ramones single to enter the _Billboard_ charts (albeit only as high as number 81): "[Sheena Is a Punk Rocker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheena_Is_a_Punk_Rocker "Sheena Is a Punk Rocker")". The follow-up single, "Rockaway Beach", reached number 66—the highest any Ramones single would ever reach in America. On December 31, 1977, the Ramones recorded _[It's Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_Alive\_(Ramones\_album) "It's Alive (Ramones album)")_, a live concert double album, at the [Rainbow Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow_Theatre "Rainbow Theatre") in London, which was released in April 1979 (the title is a reference to the [1974 horror film of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's_Alive_(1974_film) "It's Alive (1974 film)")).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-54)

### Transitional period (1978–1983)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Transitional period (1978–1983)")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Joeyramone.jpg/250px-Joeyramone.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Joeyramone.jpg)

Joey Ramone, c. 1980

Tommy, tired of touring, left the band in early 1978. He continued as the Ramones' record producer under his birth name of Erdelyi. His position as drummer was filled by [Marc Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marky_Ramone "Marky Ramone"), who had been a member of the early 1970s hard rock band [Dust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_(band) "Dust (band)"), [Wayne County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jayne_County "Jayne County"),[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-55) and the pioneering punk group [Richard Hell and the Voidoids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Hell_and_the_Voidoids "Richard Hell and the Voidoids").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-56) Bell adopted the name Marky Ramone. Later that year, the band released their fourth studio album, and first with Marky, _[Road to Ruin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road\_to\_Ruin\_(Ramones\_album) "Road to Ruin (Ramones album)")_. The album, co-produced by Tommy with [Ed Stasium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Stasium "Ed Stasium"), included some new sounds such as acoustic guitar, several ballads, and the band's first two recorded songs longer than three minutes. It failed to reach the [_Billboard_ Top 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Top_100 "Billboard Top 100"). However, "[I Wanna Be Sedated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Wanna_Be_Sedated "I Wanna Be Sedated")", which appeared both on the album and as a single, would become one of the band's best-known songs.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-57) The artwork on the album's cover was done by _Punk_ magazine cofounder [John Holmstrom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Holmstrom "John Holmstrom").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-58)

After the band's movie debut in [Roger Corman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Corman "Roger Corman")'s _[Rock 'n' Roll High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock\_'n'\_Roll\_High\_School "Rock 'n' Roll High School")_ (1979), producer [Phil Spector](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Spector "Phil Spector") became interested in the Ramones and produced their fifth album _[End of the Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End\_of\_the\_Century "End of the Century")_ (1980). There is a long-disputed rumor that during the recording sessions in Los Angeles, Spector held Dee Dee at gunpoint, forcing him to repeatedly play a riff.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-59) Although it was to be the highest-charting album in the band's history—reaching number 44 in the United States and number 14 in Great Britain—Johnny made clear that he favored the band's more aggressive punk material: "_End of the Century_ was just watered-down Ramones. It's not the real Ramones."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-60) This stance was also conveyed by the title and track selection of the compilation album Johnny later oversaw, _[Loud, Fast Ramones: Their Toughest Hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loud,\_Fast\_Ramones:\_Their\_Toughest\_Hits "Loud, Fast Ramones: Their Toughest Hits")_. Despite these reservations, Johnny did concede that some of Spector's work with the band had merit, saying "It really worked when he got to a slower song like '[Danny Says](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Says "Danny Says")'—the production really worked tremendously. 'Rock 'N' Roll Radio' is really good. For the harder stuff, it didn't work as well."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-jrst-61) The string-laden [Ronettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronettes "Ronettes") cover "[Baby, I Love You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baby,_I_Love_You "Baby, I Love You")" released as a single, became the band's biggest hit in Great Britain, reaching number 8 on the charts.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-telegraph-62)

_[Pleasant Dreams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pleasant\_Dreams "Pleasant Dreams")_, the band's sixth album, was released in 1981. It continued the trend established by _End of the Century_, taking the band further from the raw punk sound of its early records. As described by _[Trouser Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trouser\_Press "Trouser Press")_, the album, produced by [Graham Gouldman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Gouldman "Graham Gouldman") of UK pop act [10cc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10cc "10cc"), moved the Ramones "away from their pioneering minimalism into heavy metal territory."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-TP533-63) Johnny would contend in retrospect that this direction was a record company decision, a continued futile attempt to get airplay on American radio.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-mtvbio-64) While _Pleasant Dreams_ reached number 58 on the U.S. chart, its two singles failed to register at all.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-65)

_[Subterranean Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subterranean\_Jungle "Subterranean Jungle")_, produced by [Ritchie Cordell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ritchie_Cordell "Ritchie Cordell") and Glen Kolotkin, was released in 1983.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-66) According to _Trouser Press_, it brought the band "back to where they once belonged: junky '60s pop adjusted for current tastes", which among other things meant "easing off the breakneck rhythm that was once Ramones dogma."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-TP533-63) Billy Rogers, who had performed with [Johnny Thunders and the Heartbreakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Heartbreakers "The Heartbreakers"), played drums on the album's second single, a cover of [the Chambers Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chambers_Brothers "The Chambers Brothers")' "[Time Has Come Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_Has_Come_Today "Time Has Come Today")", becoming the only song showing three different drummers: Rogers on recording, Marky on album credits and Richie on video clip.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-manifesto-67) Johnny stated that he was "kinda disappointed" with _Subterranean Jungle_ because he felt it was "too melodic, too "pop", and too commercial" like _End of the Century_ and _Pleasant Dreams_.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-:0-68)_Subterranean Jungle_ peaked at number 83 in the United States—it would be the last album by the band to crack the _Billboard_ Top 100.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-69)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-70) In 2002, Rhino Records released a new version of it with seven bonus tracks.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-71)

### Shuffling members (1983–1989)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Shuffling members (1983–1989)")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Ramones_1983_b.jpg/250px-Ramones_1983_b.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ramones_1983_b.jpg)

Joey and Dee Dee Ramone performing in Seattle in 1983

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/Ramones_em_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_em_1987.jpg/250px-Ramones_em_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_em_1987.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ramones_em_S%C3%A3o_Paulo_em_1987.jpg)

Ramones performing in São Paulo in 1987

After the release of _Subterranean Jungle_, Marky was fired from the band due to his alcoholism.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-72)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-:0-68) He was replaced by Richard Reinhardt, who adopted the name [Richie Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richie_Ramone "Richie Ramone"). [Joey Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Ramone "Joey Ramone") remarked that "[Richie] saved the band as far as I'm concerned. He's the greatest thing to happen to the Ramones. He put the spirit back in the band."[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-73) Richie is the only Ramones drummer to sing lead vocals on Ramones songs, including "(You) Can't Say Anything Nice" as well as the unreleased "Elevator Operator". Joey Ramone commented, "Richie's very talented and he's very diverse ... He really strengthened the band a hundred percent because he sings backing tracks, he sings lead, and he sings with Dee Dee's stuff. In the past, it was always just me singing for the most part."[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-74) Richie was also the only drummer to be the sole composer of Ramones songs including their hit "[Somebody Put Something in My Drink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somebody_Put_Something_in_My_Drink "Somebody Put Something in My Drink")" as well as "Smash You", "Humankind", "I'm Not Jesus", "I Know Better Now" and "(You) Can't Say Anything Nice". Joey Ramone supported Richie's songwriting contributions: "I encouraged Richie to write songs. I figured it would make him feel more a part of the group, because we never let anybody else write our songs."[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-75)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-76) Richie's composition, "Somebody Put Something in My Drink", remained a staple in the Ramones set list until their last show in 1996 and was included in the album _Loud, Fast Ramones: Their Toughest Hits_.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-77) The eight-song bonus disc, _The Ramones Smash You: Live'85_, is also named after Richie's composition "Smash You".

The first album the Ramones recorded with Richie was _[Too Tough to Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too\_Tough\_to\_Die "Too Tough to Die")_ in 1984, with Tommy Erdelyi and Ed Stasium returning as producers. The album marked a shift to something like the band's original sound. In the description of Allmusic's [Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine"), the "rhythms are back up to jackhammer speed and the songs are down to short, terse statements."[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-78)

The band's only release of 1985 was the British single "[Bonzo Goes to Bitburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonzo_Goes_to_Bitburg "Bonzo Goes to Bitburg")"; though it was available in the United States only as an import, it was played widely on American college radio.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-79) The song was written, primarily by Joey, in protest of [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")'s visit to a German military cemetery, which included graves of [Waffen-SS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waffen-SS "Waffen-SS") soldiers.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-rivadavia-80) Retitled "My Brain Is Hanging Upside Down (Bonzo Goes to Bitburg)", the song appeared on the band's ninth studio album, _[Animal Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal\_Boy "Animal Boy")_ (1986). Produced by [Jean Beauvoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Beauvoir "Jean Beauvoir"), formerly a member of the [Plasmatics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plasmatics "Plasmatics"), the album was characterized by a _Rolling Stone_ reviewer as "nonstop primal fuzz pop".[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-81) Making it his pick for "album of the week", _[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_York\_Times "New York Times")_ critic [Jon Pareles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Pareles "Jon Pareles") wrote that the Ramones "speak up for outcasts and disturbed individuals".[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-82)

The following year the band recorded their last album with Richie, _[Halfway to Sanity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halfway\_to\_Sanity "Halfway to Sanity")_. Richie left in August 1987 after financial conflicts with Johnny that centered around him being refused a small percentage of the merchandising money, which had been requested based on his tenure with the band and their use of his name and image.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-film-83)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-84) Richie was replaced by [Clem Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clem_Burke "Clem Burke") from [Blondie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blondie_(band) "Blondie (band)"), which was disbanded at the time. According to Johnny, the performances with Burke—who adopted the name Elvis Ramone—were a disaster. He was fired after two performances (August 28 and 29, 1987) because his drumming could not keep up with the rest of the band.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-film-83) In September, Marky, now clean and sober, returned to the band.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-punkbands-23)

In December 1988, the Ramones recorded material for their eleventh studio album, and what was originally intended to be a "comeback" for the band,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-85)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-86)_[Brain Drain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain\_Drain\_(album) "Brain Drain (album)")_ was co-produced by Beauvoir, Rey, and [Bill Laswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Laswell "Bill Laswell"). However, the bass parts were done by Daniel Rey and [the Dictators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dictators "The Dictators")' [Andy Shernoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Shernoff "Andy Shernoff"). Dee Dee Ramone would only record the additional vocals on the album citing that members of the band (including himself) were going through personal troubles and changes to the point where he did not want to be in the band anymore. Although it received mixed reviews upon its release in May 1989, the album included the band's highest-charting hit in the US, "[Pet Sematary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet_Sematary_(song) "Pet Sematary (song)")".[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-modernrock-87)

Despite not wanting to be in the band anymore, Dee Dee (who was sober by this point) was present for the world tour for _Brain Drain_ and played his last show with the Ramones on July 5, 1989, at One Step Beyond in [Santa Clara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Clara,_California "Santa Clara, California").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-88) He was replaced by Christopher Joseph Ward ([C. J. Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._J._Ramone "C. J. Ramone")), who performed with the band until it disbanded. Dee Dee initially pursued a brief career as a rapper under the name Dee Dee King. He quickly returned to punk rock and formed several bands, in much the same vein as the Ramones. He also continued to write songs for the Ramones, but never rejoined the band.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-dee-dee-mtv-obit-89)

### Final years (1990–1996)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Final years (1990–1996)")]

The band fulfilled their contract with Sire Records in 1991 after being on the label for over a decade and a half, ending with the release of _[Loco Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loco\_Live "Loco Live")_. After leaving Sire Records, [Brett Gurewitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Gurewitz "Brett Gurewitz") of [Bad Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Religion "Bad Religion") offered to sign the band to his label [Epitaph Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epitaph_Records "Epitaph Records"), even traveling to a concert in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") and begging Joey and Johnny. Meanwhile, Stormy Shepard from Leave Home Bookings (who was booking then-up-and-coming bands on Epitaph like [the Offspring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Offspring "The Offspring") and [NOFX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOFX "NOFX"))[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-90) negotiated with the Ramones: "I'll put you on tour with these bands that are huge now. They're your fans; you can do whatever you want. You'll be playing in front of kids who like this style of music." At the same time, the band's manager, Gary Kurfurst had just worked out a deal where he was going to get his own record label, [Radioactive Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_Records "Radioactive Records"). When C. J. Ramone heard Johnny talking about signing to Kurfirst's label, he questioned: "Johnny, you've run this band for years. You carried it all yourself. I don't understand how you don't see the conflict of interest in signing to your manager's label. Just in terms of business, I don't understand how you don't see that. You're really throwing away the last few years of your career. Those Epitaph guys grew up listening to you. They will do anything to give you the business success you never had. Your manager will do the same thing he always has. He's going to throw his stuff out there. You're going to break through without anyone's support and you're going to face the rest of your career the way it's been up until now." Johnny replied: "When you have as many years in the business as I do, then you can make the decisions."

By Johnny's decision, the group ended up signing a new contract with Radioactive Records at the end of that year, the Ramones were soon able to start on sessions for what would become _[Mondo Bizarro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mondo\_Bizarro "Mondo Bizarro")_ (1992),[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-91)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-92)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-93) which saw them reunited with producer Ed Stasium.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-mondo-94) Anticipated as a "comeback" for the band after years of decline in popularity,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-95)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-96) the album was certified Gold in Brazil after selling 100,000 copies, being the first Gold certification the Ramones were ever awarded,[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-97)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-98)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-99) while its lead single "[Poison Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poison_Heart "Poison Heart")" was another top ten hit in the US for the band.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-modernrock-87)_[Acid Eaters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid\_Eaters "Acid Eaters")_, consisting entirely of cover songs, came out in 1993.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-acid-100) That same year, the Ramones were featured in the animated television series _[The Simpsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons "The Simpsons")_, providing music and voices for animated versions of themselves in the episode "[Rosebud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosebud_(The_Simpsons) "Rosebud (The Simpsons)")",[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-101) marking the series' first guest appearance by a punk band.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-102) Executive producer [David Mirkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Mirkin "David Mirkin") described the Ramones as "gigantic, obsessive _Simpsons_ fans".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-103) Marky later called their appearance "a career highlight".[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-104)

In 1995, the Ramones released their fourteenth and final studio album _[¡Adios Amigos!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adios\_Amigos\_(Ramones\_album) "Adios Amigos (Ramones album)")_ and announced that they would be disbanding the following year.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-105)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Adios-106) Its sales were unremarkable, garnering it just two weeks on the lower end of the _Billboard_ chart.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-adiosbillboard-107) The band spent late 1995 on what was promoted as a farewell tour. However, they accepted an offer to appear in the sixth [Lollapalooza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lollapalooza "Lollapalooza") festival, which toured around the United States during the following summer.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Beow%C3%BClf-108) After the Lollapalooza tour's conclusion, the Ramones played their final show on August 6, 1996, at the Palace in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood,_Los_Angeles "Hollywood, Los Angeles"). A recording of the concert was later released on video and CD as _[We're Outta Here!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're\_Outta\_Here! "We're Outta Here!")_. In addition to a reappearance by Dee Dee, the show featured several guests including [Motörhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mot%C3%B6rhead "Motörhead")'s [Lemmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemmy "Lemmy"), [Pearl Jam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Jam "Pearl Jam")'s [Eddie Vedder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddie_Vedder "Eddie Vedder"), [Soundgarden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soundgarden "Soundgarden")'s [Chris Cornell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Cornell "Chris Cornell") and [Ben Shepherd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Shepherd "Ben Shepherd"), and [Rancid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rancid_(band) "Rancid (band)")'s [Tim Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Armstrong "Tim Armstrong") and [Lars Frederiksen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lars_Frederiksen "Lars Frederiksen").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Schinder559-3)

### Aftermath and deaths of members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Aftermath and deaths of members")]

On July 20, 1999, Dee Dee, Johnny, Joey, Tommy, Marky, and C. J. appeared together at the [Virgin Megastore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_Megastore "Virgin Megastore") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") for an autograph signing. This was the last occasion on which the original four members of the group appeared together. Joey and Marky, who had been involved in a feud, buried the hatchet and made up on live radio on _[The Howard Stern Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Howard\_Stern\_Show "The Howard Stern Show")_ that same year.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-109) Joey, who had been diagnosed with [lymphoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lymphoma "Lymphoma") in 1995, died of the illness in New York on April 15, 2001.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-AP-4)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-110) Tommy, Richie and C. J. were the only former bandmates to attend his funeral.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-112)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-theaquarian-113) Joey and Richie had a close friendship during their time together in the band and the latter expressed sadness over not being able to reconnect with Joey before his death.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-theaquarian-113)

On March 18, 2002, the Ramones were inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame"), which specifically named Dee Dee, Johnny, Joey, Tommy, and Marky. At the ceremony, the surviving inductees spoke on behalf of the band. Johnny spoke first, thanking the band's fans and blessing [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") and his presidency, and America. Tommy spoke next, saying how honored the band felt, but how much it would have meant for Joey. Dee Dee humorously congratulated and thanked himself, while Marky thanked Tommy for influencing his drum style. [Green Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Day "Green Day") played "Teenage Lobotomy", "Rockaway Beach", and "[Blitzkrieg Bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blitzkrieg_Bop "Blitzkrieg Bop")" as a tribute, demonstrating the Ramones' continuing influence on later rock musicians. The ceremony was one of Dee Dee's last public appearances, as he was found dead on June 5, 2002, from a [heroin overdose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opioid_overdose "Opioid overdose").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-nytimes-5)

The documentary film _[End of the Century: The Story of the Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End\_of\_the\_Century:\_The\_Story\_of\_the\_Ramones "End of the Century: The Story of the Ramones")_ came out in 2004. Johnny, who had been diagnosed with [prostate cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostate_cancer "Prostate cancer") in 1999, died on September 15, 2004, in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), shortly after the film's release.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Sisario-6) On the same day as Johnny's death, the world's first [Ramones Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones_Museum "Ramones Museum") opened its doors to the public. Located in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), Germany, the museum features more than 300 items of memorabilia, including a pair of stage-worn jeans from Johnny, a stage-worn glove from Joey, Marky's sneakers, and C. J.'s stage-worn bass strap.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-114) On October 8, 2004, [Tommy Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Ramone "Tommy Ramone"), [C. J. Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._J._Ramone "C. J. Ramone"), Clem Burke, and [Daniel Rey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Rey "Daniel Rey") performed together in the "Ramones Beat on Cancer" concert.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-115) Burke, who briefly replaced Richie in the Ramones in 1987, died on April 6, 2025, after a battle with cancer, making him the first non-original member of the band to die.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-116)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-117)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-118)

## Conflicts between members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Conflicts between members")]

Tension between [Joey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Ramone "Joey Ramone") and [Johnny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Ramone "Johnny Ramone") colored much of the Ramones' career. The pair were [politically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politically "Politically") antagonistic, with Joey being a [liberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_liberalism_in_the_United_States "Modern liberalism in the United States") and Johnny a [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States "Conservatism in the United States").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-119) Their personalities also clashed: Johnny spent two years in [military school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_school "Military school") and lived by a strict code of [self-discipline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-discipline "Self-discipline"),[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-120) while Joey struggled with [obsessive–compulsive disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obsessive%E2%80%93compulsive_disorder "Obsessive–compulsive disorder") and [alcoholism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholism "Alcoholism").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-121)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-122) In the early 1980s, Linda Danielle began a relationship with Johnny after having already been romantically involved with Joey, who had reportedly accused Johnny of "stealing" his girlfriend. This incident is believed to have been the inspiration behind "[The KKK Took My Baby Away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_KKK_Took_My_Baby_Away "The KKK Took My Baby Away")".[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-ref1-123) Consequently, despite their continued professional relationship, Joey and Johnny had become aloof from each other.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Sisario-6) Johnny did not contact Joey before his death, although he said that he was [depressed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_(mood) "Depression (mood)") for "the whole week" after his death.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-film-83)
