[Dee Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dee_Dee_Ramone "Dee Dee Ramone")'s [bipolar disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipolar_disorder "Bipolar disorder") and repeated relapses into [drug addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_addiction "Drug addiction") also caused significant strains.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-124) Tommy would also leave the band after being "physically threatened by Johnny, treated with contempt by Dee Dee, and all but ignored by Joey."[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Beeber-125) As new members joined over the years, disbursement and the band's image frequently became matters of serious dispute.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-126) The tensions among the group members were not kept secret from the public as was heard on _[The Howard Stern Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Howard\_Stern\_Show "The Howard Stern Show")_ in 1997, where during the interview [Marky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marky_Ramone "Marky Ramone") and Joey got into a fight about their respective drinking habits.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-127)

Political conflicts also existed between Marky and [C. J.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._J._Ramone "C. J. Ramone"), the latter of whom described it as, "[Marky] made fun of everything conservative and traditional, and I made fun of everything political, both conservative and liberal."[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-markprindle_markyramone-i-128) A year after the Ramones' breakup, Marky Ramone made disparaging remarks against C. J. in the press, saying he couldn't stand touring with him, and calling him a "[bigot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bigot "Bigot")",[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-129) a statement he would reiterate a decade later.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-markprindle_markyramone-i-128) C. J. would later respond that he was unsure as to why Marky would make negative comments against him in the press, though he denied that it had anything to do with him marrying Marky's niece. He also denied being a bigot.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-130) Many years later, C. J. lamented that despite being the two surviving members of arguably the Ramones' most commercially successful era, and despite reaching out a few times to join him on stage, he and Marky were no longer in contact.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-131)

## Artistry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Artistry")]

### Musical style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Musical style")]

The Ramones' loud, fast, straightforward musical style was influenced by [pop music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music") that the band members grew up listening to in the 1950s and 1960s, including [classic rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_rock "Classic rock") groups such as [Buddy Holly and the Crickets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddy_Holly_and_the_Crickets "Buddy Holly and the Crickets"), [the Beach Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beach_Boys "The Beach Boys"), [the Who](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Who "The Who"), [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles"), [the Kinks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Kinks "The Kinks"), [Led Zeppelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Led_Zeppelin "Led Zeppelin"), [the Rolling Stones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rolling_Stones "The Rolling Stones"), [the Doors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Doors "The Doors") and [Creedence Clearwater Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creedence_Clearwater_Revival "Creedence Clearwater Revival"); [bubblegum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubblegum_music "Bubblegum music") acts like the [1910 Fruitgum Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1910_Fruitgum_Company "1910 Fruitgum Company") and [Ohio Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_Express "Ohio Express"); and girl groups such as [the Ronettes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ronettes "The Ronettes") and [the Shangri-Las](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Shangri-Las "The Shangri-Las"). They also drew on the harder rock sound of the [MC5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MC5 "MC5"), Black Sabbath,[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-132)[the Stooges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Stooges "The Stooges") and the [New York Dolls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Dolls "New York Dolls"), now known as seminal [proto-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-punk "Proto-punk") bands.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-133) The Ramones' style was in part a reaction against the heavily produced, often bombastic music that dominated the pop charts in the 1970s. "We decided to start our own group because we were bored with everything we heard," Joey once explained. "In 1974 everything was tenth-generation [Elton John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_John "Elton John"), or overproduced, or just junk. Everything was long jams, long [guitar solos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guitar_solos "Guitar solos").... We missed music like it used to be."[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-134) Ira Robbins and Scott Isler of _[Trouser Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trouser\_Press "Trouser Press")_ describe the result:

> With just four chords and one manic tempo, [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City")'s Ramones blasted open the clogged arteries of mid-'70s rock, reanimating the music. Their genius was to recapture the short/simple aesthetic from which pop had strayed, adding a caustic sense of [trash-culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trash_culture "Trash culture") humor and minimalist rhythm guitar sound.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-TP-135)

As leaders in the [punk rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock") scene, the Ramones' music is strongly identified with that label.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-mtvbio-64) It has been noted that their recordings also helped the subgenre [pop-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-punk "Pop-punk") to develop.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-136)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-137)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-punkco-138) Some have described certain Ramones songs as [power pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_pop "Power pop").[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-zivkovic-139)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-powerpophof-140)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-happyfamily-141) Starting in the 1980s, the band sometimes veered into [hardcore punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcore_punk "Hardcore punk") territory, as can be heard on albums such as _[Too Tough to Die](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Too\_Tough\_to\_Die "Too Tough to Die")_.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-TP-135)

On stage, the band adopted a focused approach directly intended to increase the audience's concert experience. [Johnny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Ramone "Johnny Ramone")'s instructions to [C. J.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._J._Ramone "C. J. Ramone") when preparing for his first live performances with the group were to play facing the audience, to stand with the bass slung low between spread legs, and to walk forward to the front of stage at the same time as he did. Johnny was not a fan of guitarists who performed facing their drummer, amplifier, or other band members.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-142)

### Visual imagery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Visual imagery")]

The Ramones' art and visual imagery complemented the themes of their music and performance. The members adopted a uniform look of long hair, [leather jackets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leather_jackets "Leather jackets"), T-shirts, torn jeans, and [sneakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sneakers "Sneakers"). This fashion emphasized [minimalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimalism "Minimalism")—a powerful influence on the [New York punk scene of the 1970s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock "Punk rock")—and reflected the band's short, simple songs.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-CS67-143)[Tommy Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Ramone "Tommy Ramone") recalled that, musically and visually, "We were influenced by comic books, movies, the [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol") scene, and [avant-garde films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avant-garde_films "Avant-garde films"). I was a big _[Mad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mad\_(magazine) "Mad (magazine)")_ magazine fan myself."[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-CS67-143)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/57/Ramones_logo.jpg/250px-Ramones_logo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ramones_logo.jpg)

The band's logo, based on the [seal of the president of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_of_the_president_of_the_United_States "Seal of the president of the United States")

The band's logo was created by [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") artist [Arturo Vega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Vega "Arturo Vega"), with guidance from the Ramones. Vega, a longtime friend, had allowed [Joey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_Ramone "Joey Ramone") and [Dee Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dee_Dee_Ramone "Dee Dee Ramone") to move into his loft.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-McCain_&_McNeil,_211-144) He produced the band's T-shirts—their main source of income—basing most of the images on a black-and-white self-portrait photograph he had taken of his American bald eagle belt buckle, which appeared on the back sleeve of the Ramones' first album.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-B40-145) He was inspired to create the band's logo after a trip to [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."):

> I saw them as the ultimate all-American band. To me, they reflected the American character in general—an almost childish innocent aggression.... I thought, "The Great [Seal of the President of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seal_of_the_president_of_the_United_States "Seal of the president of the United States")" would be perfect for the Ramones, with the [eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eagle "Eagle") holding arrows—to symbolize strength and the aggression that would be used against whomever dares to attack us—and an olive branch, offered to those who want to be friendly. But we decided to change it a little bit. Instead of the olive branch, we had an apple tree branch, since the Ramones were American as [apple pie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_pie "Apple pie"). And since Johnny was such a [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") fanatic, we had the eagle hold a [baseball bat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball_bat "Baseball bat") instead of the Great Seal's arrows.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-B40-145)

The scroll in the eagle's beak originally read "Look out below", but this was soon changed to "Hey ho let's go" after the opening lyrics of the band's first single, "[Blitzkrieg Bop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blitzkrieg_Bop "Blitzkrieg Bop")". The arrowheads on the shield came from a design on a polyester shirt Vega had bought. "Ramones" was spelled out in block capitals above the logo using plastic stick-on letters.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Bessman,_211-28) Where the presidential emblem read "Seal of the President of the United States" clockwise in the border around the eagle, Vega placed the pseudonyms of the band members: [Johnny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Ramone "Johnny Ramone"), Joey, Dee Dee, and Tommy. Over the years the names in the border would change as the band's line-up fluctuated.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-146)

"It's the American presidential seal—anyone can use it," said [Marky Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marky_Ramone "Marky Ramone") of the logo's ubiquity. "We share the [royalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royalty_payment "Royalty payment") on the t-shirt and on the merchandise. A lot of the kids wearing that shirt might not even have heard of the Ramones' music. I guess if you have the shirt, your curiosity might bring you to buy the music. Whatever, it is a strange phenomenon."[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-147)

## Legacy and influence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Legacy and influence")]

Never a widely popular band in the United States while active, [Gene Simmons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Simmons "Gene Simmons") of [Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_(band) "Kiss (band)") observed of the Ramones, "They have [one gold record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones_(album) "Ramones (album)") to their name. They never played arenas; couldn't sell them out... [i]t doesn't mean they weren't great. It means the masses didn't care."[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-148)

The Ramones would have a broad and lasting influence on the development of [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music"). Music historian [Jon Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Savage "Jon Savage") writes of their [debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones_(album) "Ramones (album)") that "it remains one of the few records that changed pop forever."[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-149) As described by [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") critic [Stephen Thomas Erlewine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Thomas_Erlewine "Stephen Thomas Erlewine"), "The band's first four albums set the blueprint for punk, especially American punk and hardcore, for the next two decades."[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-150)_Trouser Press_'s Robbins and Isler similarly wrote that the Ramones "not only spearheaded the original new wave/punk movement, but also drew the blueprint for subsequent hardcore punk bands".[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-TP-135) Punk journalist Phil Strongman writes, "In purely _musical_ terms, the Ramones, in attempting to re-create the excitement of pre-Dolby rock, were to cast a huge shadow—they had fused a blueprint for much of the indie future."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-St62-29) Writing for _[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate\_(magazine) "Slate (magazine)")_ in 2001, [Douglas Wolk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_Wolk "Douglas Wolk") described the Ramones as "easily the most influential group of the last 30 years".[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-151)

### Punk and hardcore

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Punk and hardcore")]

Locally, several musicians who would play in [New York hardcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_hardcore "New York hardcore") bands cite the Ramones as an influence. These include members of the [Beastie Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beastie_Boys "Beastie Boys"),[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_][Gorilla Biscuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorilla_Biscuits "Gorilla Biscuits"),[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-152)[Heart Attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heart_Attack_(band) "Heart Attack (band)"),[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-153) the [Misfits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misfits_(band) "Misfits (band)"),[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-154)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-155) and [the Mob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mob_(American_hardcore_band) "The Mob (American hardcore band)").[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-156)[Roger Miret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Miret "Roger Miret") of [Agnostic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnostic_Front "Agnostic Front") has stated that _Leave Home_ was the first album he bought with his own money.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-157) They were also influential to early [Boston punk and hardcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_hardcore "Boston hardcore") groups, [Mission of Burma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_of_Burma "Mission of Burma") drummer [Peter Prescott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Prescott_(musician) "Peter Prescott (musician)") has highlighted the Ramones self-titled debut as their foremost influence, while [SSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SSD_(band) "SSD (band)") guitarist Al Barile was inspired to play guitar after hearing Johnny Ramone.[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-158)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-159) In [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), seminal [D.C. hardcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D.C._hardcore "D.C. hardcore") band [Bad Brains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Brains "Bad Brains") took their name from a Ramones song, and [Henry Rollins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Rollins "Henry Rollins") described seeing a Ramones live set, "as full-on a live experience as I have ever had and almost ruined me for going to other shows."[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-160)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-161)

Canada's first major punk scenes in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto") and in [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia")'s [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_British_Columbia "Victoria, British Columbia") and [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), such as [Teenage Head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teenage_Head_(band) "Teenage Head (band)"),[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-162)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-163)[Nomeansno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nomeansno "Nomeansno"), and [D.O.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D.O.A._(band) "D.O.A. (band)"), were also heavily influenced by the Ramones.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-LW-49)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-164) While Ramones concerts and recordings also influenced many musicians central to the development of [California punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punk_rock_in_California "Punk rock in California"), including [Greg Ginn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Ginn "Greg Ginn") of [Black Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Flag_(band) "Black Flag (band)"),[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-165)[Jello Biafra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jello_Biafra "Jello Biafra") and [East Bay Ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Bay_Ray "East Bay Ray") of the [Dead Kennedys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Kennedys "Dead Kennedys"),[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-166)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-167)[Mike Ness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ness "Mike Ness") of [Social Distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Distortion "Social Distortion"),[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-168)[Brett Gurewitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brett_Gurewitz "Brett Gurewitz") of [Bad Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Religion "Bad Religion"),[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-169)[Mike Muir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Muir "Mike Muir") of [Suicidal Tendencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicidal_Tendencies "Suicidal Tendencies"),[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-170)[Fat Mike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fat_Mike "Fat Mike") of [NOFX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NOFX "NOFX"),[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-171) and members of the [Descendents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Descendents "Descendents"),[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-172)[the Zeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Zeros_(American_band) "The Zeros (American band)"),[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-173) and [the Dickies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dickies "The Dickies").[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-174)

The Ramones' [eponymous debut album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones_(album) "Ramones (album)") had an outsized effect relative to its modest sales, particularly in the [UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). According to [Generation X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_X_(band) "Generation X (band)") bassist [Tony James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_James_(musician) "Tony James (musician)"), "Everybody went up three gears the day they got that first Ramones album. Punk rock—that rama-lama super fast stuff—is totally down to the Ramones. Bands were just playing in an [MC5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MC5 "MC5") groove until then."[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-175) His bandmate, [Billy Idol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Idol "Billy Idol"), reiterated this saying that except for the [Sex Pistols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_Pistols "Sex Pistols"), every London punk band started speeding up their music up after hearing the Ramones.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-176) While Sex Pistols drummer [Paul Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Cook "Paul Cook") denied a musical influence, he credits the release of the first Ramones album as motivating the Pistols.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-177)

The Ramones' two July 1976 shows, like their debut album, are seen as having a significant impact on the style of many of the newly formed British punk acts—as one observer put it, "instantly nearly every band speeded up".[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-178) The Ramones' first British concert, at London's Roundhouse music venue, was held on July 4, 1976, the [United States Bicentennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Bicentennial "United States Bicentennial").[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-179) The Sex Pistols were playing in [Sheffield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheffield "Sheffield") that evening, supported by [the Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Clash "The Clash"), making their public debut. The next night, members of both bands attended the Ramones' gig at the Dingwall's club. Ramones manager Danny Fields recalls a conversation between Johnny Ramone and Clash bassist [Paul Simonon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Simonon "Paul Simonon") (which he mislocates at the Roundhouse): "Johnny asked him, 'What do you do? Are you in a band?' Paul said, 'Well, we just rehearse. We call ourselves the Clash but we're not good enough.' Johnny said, 'Wait till you see us—we stink, we're lousy, we can't play. Just get out there and do it.'"[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-180) Another band whose members saw the Ramones perform on the 4th, [the Damned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Damned_(band) "The Damned (band)"), played [their first show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_at_the_100_Club_(The_Damned_album) "Live at the 100 Club (The Damned album)") two days later.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-181)

Other U.K. punk bands who were influenced during this period include [Chelsea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_(band) "Chelsea (band)"),[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-182)[the Lurkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Lurkers "The Lurkers"),[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-183)[the Undertones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Undertones "The Undertones"),[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-184) and [The Vibrators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vibrators "The Vibrators").[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-185)[Jimmy Pursey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Pursey "Jimmy Pursey") of [Sham 69](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sham_69 "Sham 69") has said that he considers the Ramones his band's "only blueprint".[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-186) The central [fanzine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanzine "Fanzine") of the early UK punk scene, _[Sniffin' Glue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sniffin'\_Glue "Sniffin' Glue")_, was named after the song "Now I Wanna Sniff Some Glue", which appeared on the debut LP.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-DG-187)

The Ramones' pop-influenced style of punk rock has been credited for paving the way for the birth of [pop-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop-punk "Pop-punk"),[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-188) being cited as an influence by those of [Green Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Day "Green Day"), [the Offspring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Offspring "The Offspring"), [Blink-182](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blink-182 "Blink-182"),[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-189)[Fall Out Boy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_Out_Boy "Fall Out Boy"),[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-190)[New Found Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Found_Glory "New Found Glory"),[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-191) and [Alkaline Trio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaline_Trio "Alkaline Trio").[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-192) Green Day frontman [Billie Joe Armstrong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billie_Joe_Armstrong "Billie Joe Armstrong") named his son Joey in homage to Joey Ramone, and drummer [Tré Cool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tr%C3%A9_Cool "Tré Cool") named his daughter Ramona.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-193) The [Riverdales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverdales "Riverdales"), who Armstrong produced, emulated the sound of the Ramones throughout their career.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-194)

### Other genres

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Other genres")]

The Ramones also influenced musicians associated with genres outside of punk, such as [heavy metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_metal_music "Heavy metal music"). Their influence on metal gave birth to the punk-metal "fusion" genre of [thrash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrash_metal "Thrash metal"). [Metallica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallica "Metallica") guitarist [Kirk Hammett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirk_Hammett "Kirk Hammett"), one of the originators of thrash guitar, has described the importance of Johnny's rapid-fire guitar playing style to his own musical development.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-195)[Motörhead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mot%C3%B6rhead "Motörhead") lead singer [Lemmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lemmy "Lemmy"), a friend of the Ramones since the late 1970s, mixed the band's "Go Home Ann" in 1985. The members of Motörhead later composed the song "[R.A.M.O.N.E.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R.A.M.O.N.E.S. "R.A.M.O.N.E.S.")" as a tribute, and Lemmy performed at the final Ramones concert in 1996.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-196)[Paul Di'Anno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Di'Anno "Paul Di'Anno"), who sang on [Iron Maiden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Maiden "Iron Maiden")'s first two albums called the Ramones his "favorite band", and often performed Ramones material in his live shows.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-197)[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-198) In the realm of [alternative rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_rock "Alternative rock"), the song "[53rd & 3rd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/53rd_&_3rd_(song) "53rd & 3rd (song)")" lent its name to a British [indie pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_pop "Indie pop") label cofounded by Stephen Pastel of the Scottish band [the Pastels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pastels "The Pastels"), and [Morrissey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrissey "Morrissey"), while initially giving a negative review to the Ramones debut album, later commented, "three days after writing that Ramones piece, I realized that my love for the Ramones would out-live time itself."[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-199) In 2014, he was invited by the band's management to pick the tracks for a compilation that became _[Morrissey Curates The Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morrissey\_Curates\_The\_Ramones "Morrissey Curates The Ramones")._[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-200)

### Tribute albums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Tribute albums")]

In April 2009, _Spin_ writer Mark Prindle observed that the Ramones had to date "inspired a jaw-dropping 48(at least!) full-length tribute records".[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-PrindleTributes-212) The first Ramones tribute album featuring multiple performers was released in 1991: _[Gabba Gabba Hey: A Tribute to the Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabba\_Gabba\_Hey:\_A\_Tribute\_to\_the\_Ramones "Gabba Gabba Hey: A Tribute to the Ramones")_ includes tracks by well-known [major label](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_label "Major label") punk acts [L7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L7_(band) "L7 (band)") and [Bad Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Religion "Bad Religion").[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-gaba-213) In 2001, Dee Dee made a guest appearance on one track of _[Ramones Maniacs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones\_Maniacs "Ramones Maniacs")_, a multi-artist cover of the entire _[Ramones Mania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones\_Mania "Ramones Mania")_ compilation album. _[The Song Ramones the Same](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Song\_Ramones\_the\_Same "The Song Ramones the Same")_, which came out the following year, includes performances by [protopunk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protopunk "Protopunk") artists who influenced the Ramones like [the Dictators](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dictators "The Dictators") and [Wayne Kramer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Kramer_(guitarist) "Wayne Kramer (guitarist)"), as well as Ramones-influenced artists like [Jesse Malin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Malin "Jesse Malin").[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-214)_[We're a Happy Family: A Tribute to Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We're\_a\_Happy\_Family:\_A\_Tribute\_to\_Ramones "We're a Happy Family: A Tribute to Ramones")_, released in 2003, features several fellow Rock & Roll Hall of Famers such as [Green Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Day "Green Day"), [Metallica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallica "Metallica"), [Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiss_(band) "Kiss (band)"), [the Pretenders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pretenders "The Pretenders"), [Red Hot Chili Peppers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Hot_Chili_Peppers "Red Hot Chili Peppers"), [U2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U2 "U2"), and [Tom Waits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Waits "Tom Waits").[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-215)

Punk bands such as [Screeching Weasel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screeching_Weasel "Screeching Weasel"), [the Vindictives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Vindictives "The Vindictives"), [the Queers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Queers "The Queers"), [Parasites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parasites_(band) "Parasites (band)"), [the Mr. T Experience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mr._T_Experience "The Mr. T Experience"), [Boris the Sprinkler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_the_Sprinkler "Boris the Sprinkler"), Beatnik Termites, Tip Toppers, [Jon Cougar Concentration Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Cougar_Concentration_Camp "Jon Cougar Concentration Camp"), and McRackins have recorded cover versions of entire Ramones albums—_Ramones_, _Leave Home_, _Rocket to Russia_, _It's Alive_, _Road to Ruin_, _End of the Century_, _Pleasant Dreams_, _Subterranean Jungle_, two versions of _Too Tough to Die_, and _Halfway to Sanity_, respectively.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-PrindleTributes-212)[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-216)[The Huntingtons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Huntingtons "The Huntingtons")' _[File Under Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File\_Under\_Ramones "File Under Ramones")_ consists of Ramones covers from across the band's history.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-217)

[Shonen Knife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shonen_Knife "Shonen Knife"), an all-female trio from Osaka, Japan, was formed in 1981 as a direct result of founder-lead singer-guitarist [Naoko Yamano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naoko_Yamano "Naoko Yamano")'s instant infatuation with the music of the Ramones. In 2012, to observe the band's 30th anniversary, Shonen Knife released _[Osaka Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka\_Ramones "Osaka Ramones")_, which featured thirteen Ramones songs covered by the band.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-218) There are also many other tribute albums listed on Jari-Pekka Laitio-Ramone's site.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-219)

### Accolades

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ramones&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Accolades")]

In 2000, [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1")'s _100 Greatest Artists of Hard Rock_ ranked the group at 17 on their list.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In addition to their 2002 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, the Ramones were inducted into the [Long Island Music Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Music_Hall_of_Fame "Long Island Music Hall of Fame") in 2007.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-220) That October saw the release of a DVD set containing concert footage of the band: _[It's Alive 1974–1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_Alive\_1974%E2%80%931996 "It's Alive 1974–1996")_ includes 118 songs from 33 performances over the span of the group's career.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-221) In February 2011 the group was honored with a [Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award "Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award"). Drummers Tommy, Marky, and Richie attended the ceremony.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Sterndan-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-grammy1-14) Marky declared, "This is amazing. I never expected this. I'm sure Johnny, Joey, and Dee Dee would never have expected this."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-Sterndan-13) Richie noted that it was the first time ever that all three drummers were under the same roof, and mused that he couldn't "help thinking that [Joey] is watching us right now with a little smile on his face behind his rose-colored glasses."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-grammy1-14) On April 30, 2014, their debut album, _[Ramones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramones\_(album) "Ramones (album)")_, became certified Gold by the [Recording Industry of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recording_Industry_of_America "Recording Industry of America") (RIAA) after selling 500,000 copies, 38 years after its release.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-222)

The band members were also individually influential. [Johnny Ramone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Ramone "Johnny Ramone") was named one of [_Time_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")'s "10 Greatest Electric-Guitar Players" in 2003.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-223) That same year, he was number 16 on the "100 Greatest Guitarists of All Time" list in _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-224) On November 30, 2003, New York City unveiled a sign designating East 2nd Street at the corner of Bowery as Joey Ramone Place. The singer lived on East 2nd for a time, and the sign is near the former Bowery site of [CBGB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBGB "CBGB").[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ramones#cite_note-225)

The French animated series _[Oggy and the Cockroaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oggy\_and\_the\_Cockroaches "Oggy and the Cockroaches")_ features a trio of anthropomorphic cockroaches named after three members of the band — Joey, Marky and Dee Dee.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
